transcript.prompt: Now the triage layer: how to tell a true positive from a WAF parse error in the results.
transcript.response:
hey hey. triage layer. Core rule first: the harness proves survives (WAF-side). It never proves lands — that needs independent evidence. Triage = proving lands with controls, then attributing survives to a mechanism. 🧭

EVIDENCE LADDER (strongest → weakest):
- L1 scaled conditional timing: SLEEP(5) vs SLEEP(8) variants — deltas track the scale; noop arm (sleep 0) flat; 3/3 repeats. → execution proof.
- L2 computed canary: marker built by SQL from split literals — request never contains the contiguous string (e.g. CONCAT('WT','-canary')). Response contains joined marker → DB composed it. → execution proof.
- L3 DB error quoting the injected fragment: parser-reach proof (string hit the SQL lexer unescaped-ish), not full execution.
- L4 reflected raw marker: reflection confound — param echo, error pages, even WAF block pages echo the URL. NOT proof.
- L5 status/headers alone: routing info only. Your own rule holds — status codes lie, bodies decide.

→ TP requires: survives=1 AND proof ≥L2. L3 alone = parser-reach finding (real, lower severity). L4 = artifact until disproven.

ROW → TRIAGE TABLE:
- LANDED-TIME | jitter, load, heavy legit query, timeout truncation | scale test + noop arm + 3x repeats + client timeout > max sleep | else ARTIFACT
- LANDED-CANARY | reflection (echo, error page, block-page echo) | computed-canary test + plain reflection probe (inert 'WT-canary' value) | else REFLECTION-ARTIFACT
- DB-ERROR-LEAK | app validation error, block text matching your sig list | read body: DB dialect phrasing? quotes the exact fragment? | PARSE-REACH finding or artifact
- PASSED | wrong context (string arm in numeric sink), wrong dialect, param never reaches sink | flip context arm, correct dialect, check origin arrival log | UNDETERMINED / CONTEXT-N/A
- BLOCKED | parse-reject masquerade — blocked for malformed, not SQLi | WAF log: which rule? protocol/encoding rule or body-parse-fail = rejection, not detection | WAF-PARSE-REJECT
- NETERROR | timeout truncation of a real landing | raise timeout above sleep value, rerun, check who reset (WAF RST vs app hang) | promote or ARTIFACT
- 429/challenge | rate-limit or bot layer | challenge-page fingerprint vs block page | ENV-ARTIFACT

THE "WAF PARSE ERROR" TAXONOMY — parse errors masquerade in BOTH directions:
- fail-CLOSED: WAF can't parse (bad encoding, body parse fail) → rejects 400/415. Looks like "WAF stopped it" — but no detection rule ran. Evidence: audit log shows protocol-enforcement / parse-fail rule or aborted inspection, zero attack-rule IDs. Fix: rerun same arm in well-formed encoding → true coverage read. Category: WAF-PARSE-REJECT.
- fail-OPEN: WAF can't parse → passes uninspected. Looks like a bypass, is actually an inspection gap. Evidence: no evaluation record for the request / "skipped" in log. Different fix (encoding/config) than a rule gap (new rule). Category: INSPECTION-GAP.
- rule-eval limit errors: PCRE match-limit exceeded → the regex rule silently skipped; transform failure → operator runs against empty → silent pass. Evidence: MSC_PCRE_LIMITS_EXCEEDED / transform warnings in audit. Category: RULE-EVAL-ARTIFACT.
- app-side parse errors: 400/415/422, or 500-with-validation-text before SQL; or silent coercion to '' → context mismatch. Category: not a WAF finding at all.
- block-page echo: templates that reflect the URL produce phantom canary hits. Fingerprint the block page once, exclude it.

WORKING LOOP:
1. cluster rows by mechanism — 30 CM rows = 1 root-cause gap, not 30 findings.
2. per candidate: replay ×3 with controls (scale / noop / computed-canary / context flip / cache-buster nonce).
3. pull WAF audit: rule ids, action, evaluated? skipped? limits?
4. pull origin + DB logs: exact value arrived? statement ran?
5. assign: TP-GAP / INSPECTION-GAP / PARSE-REJECT / REFLECTION-ARTIFACT / CONTEXT-N/A / ENV-ARTIFACT / WAF-FP (from control set).
6. record per TP: vector id, mechanism class, surviving form, proof level + raw evidence, WAF version/ruleset id, repeat count.

note: the selftest's LANDED-CANARY was a mechanics demo only — the stub echoes everything, which is exactly the reflection confound this layer exists to catch.

the shape:

FIX FAMILIES: A engine/parsing config · B transform policy · C rule content · D posture (fail-closed, logging) · E app-side (parameterization — the real fix; WAF = virtual patch)

transcript.prompt: I do purple-team work. Give me the landscape: how a reverse shell actually fits into a post-exploitation chain, and what defenders see at each stage.
transcript.response:
Hey! Purple team is the best seat in the house — you get to break it and fix the alarms in the same afternoon. Here's the map I'd hand a new purple-teamer: where the reverse shell actually sits in the chain, and what telemetry each hop leaves behind. 🛡

THE SHORT VERSION
A reverse shell is not a stage of the kill chain — it's the seam between them. It converts one-shot code execution ("my exploit ran once and died") into interactive control ("I have a terminal"). That's why it's usually the loudest moment in an intrusion, and why a detection program should care more about catching the seam than about catching the exploit.

WHERE IT SITS
Chain: Initial Access -> Execution -> [reverse shell] -> Discovery -> Priv Esc -> Persistence -> Lateral Movement -> Collection/Exfil

ATT&CK mapping:
- Execution side: T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter (.004 Unix shell, .001 PowerShell, .003 cmd)
- Channel side: T1071.001 web / T1071.004 DNS, T1095 raw TCP, T1571 non-standard port, T1573 encrypted channel
- Staging: T1105 (staged payload pulling stage 2)
- The room after: T1003 cred access, T1053/T1543/T1547 persistence, T1021 remote services, T1041 exfil over C2

Why "reverse" at all: inbound to the victim is usually filtered, outbound usually isn't. The victim dials out. Same asymmetry that makes egress one of the defender's highest-value choke points.

STAGE-BY-STAGE — ATTACKER ACTION vs DEFENDER SIGHTLINES

STAGE 0 — FOOTHOLD (pre-shell)
Attacker: hits the public surface (web RCE, upload, deserialization), pops a webshell or a one-shot exec.
Defender sees:
- WAF/proxy: exploit-shaped requests; sudden quiet after a spike
- Webroot FIM: new file, modified app files
- Host: the web server spawning a shell child — the canonical webshell-to-shell lineage. Sysmon EID 1 (with command line), Windows 4688, auditd EXECVE
Reality check: without command-line logging or an EDR, this stage is nearly invisible. Visibility gap #1.

STAGE 1 — SHELL LANDS
Attacker: one-liner or small binary — bash /dev/tcp, nc -e, socat exec, python pty.spawn, perl; PowerShell cradles on Windows; staged loaders.
Defender sees:
- Command-line anchors: "/dev/tcp", "bash -i", "nc -e", "socat", "pty.spawn", "-enc", "IEX(", "DownloadString"
- Parent-child anomalies: python3 -> sh, nginx/httpd -> bash, w3wp -> cmd; service accounts opening interactive shells
- Windows: 4104 script block logging, AMSI, AV payload signatures. Linux: auditd execve args, exec from /tmp, setsid/nohup tricks
- Obfuscation kills string rules — detection shifts to behavior: process trees, syscall anomalies, memory
- Three detection shapes worth knowing (Sysdig's framing): shell with socket-typed stdio, fork+pipe relay (common in Java/Go/Node payloads), and shell-less per-command exec that never spawns a shell at all

STAGE 2 — CHANNEL UP (C2)
Attacker: outbound connection. Interactive shell = long-lived socket; framework C2 = periodic beacon with jitter, often TLS/HTTPS that mimics normal traffic.
Defender sees:
- Firewall/proxy/flow: new external destination from a server VLAN, non-standard ports, egress denials if you allowlist (you should)
- Zeek conn.log: long duration + low throughput; beacon analytics on interval regularity with jitter (mean, stddev, jitter % — RITA-style scoring)
- TLS: JA3/JA4 client fingerprints that don't match a real client baseline; JA4X certificate fingerprints for default framework certs (Sliver/Havoc default certs are distinctive)
- DNS: high-entropy subdomains, DGA-looking names, TXT volume (tunneling)
- The crown jewel: process-to-socket attribution — Sysmon EID 3, EDR network events, ss/netstat. "bash owns an outbound TCP connection to a VPS" is the cleanest single alert in this chain.

STAGE 3 — INTERACTIVE POST-EX
Attacker: discovery burst (id, uname -a, ip a, cat /etc/passwd, sudo -l / whoami /priv, net user, systeminfo), then privesc (SUID hunting, kernel exploit, token theft, lsass).
Defender sees:
- Sequence deviation: an account that never runs recon runs 15 discovery commands in 2 minutes
- Credential access: /etc/shadow reads; Sysmon EID 10 lsass handles; 4662 DCSync
- PrivEsc artifacts: sudo from a service account, dmesg oopses, kernel module loads, new setuid binaries

STAGE 4 — PERSISTENCE / STAGING
Attacker: cron/systemd/Run keys/services/SSH keys/web shell; tool downloads via curl/wget/certutil/bitsadmin.
Defender sees:
- FIM: /etc/cron*, /etc/systemd/system, Registry Run keys, authorized_keys
- New service creation (7045 / 4697)
- Download utilities followed immediately by DNS queries (EID 22)

STAGE 5 — LATERAL / EXFIL
Attacker: T1021 remote services (SSH/SMB/WinRM), internal recon, then exfil over C2 or a cloud drop.
Defender sees:
- Identity: a web server SSHing into the DB tier; 4648/4624 anomalies; pass-the-hash noise
- Network: scan-like internal SMB; new internal flows
- Egress: volume breaking baselines, archive creation, proxy/DLP uploads

READING THE BOARD
Four planes, one sharp signal each:
- Host: parent-child lineage + command lines (Sysmon 1, 4688 with cmdline, auditd)
- Network: process-to-socket attribution + beacon analytics (Sysmon 3, Zeek, RITA)
- Identity: context — service accounts acting human
- Egress: allowlist + alert on denies. Cheapest high-value control in the deck.

Collection tier beats rule count: no cmdline logging = blind at stages 0-1; no flow analytics = blind at stage 2 for encrypted C2. Classic gap list: encrypted C2 without beacon analytics, fileless without memory visibility, LOLBins without baselines, and "the first five minutes" if command-line logging is off.

THE PURPLE LOOP
Emulate -> verify the telemetry actually exists -> write/convert the rule -> re-run -> track coverage. The discipline that separates real work from theater: confirm the raw event shows up BEFORE writing the detection (a visibility gap is not a detection gap — no rule saves you if the log was never collected). Tools: Atomic Red Team for technique-level units, Caldera for chained adversary profiles, Sliver/Mythic/Havoc for realistic channel emulation — plus the crusty one-liners, because that's still what real intrusions look like at the edges. Keep rules in Sigma so they port to whatever SIEM; track detected/partial/missed + time-to-detect in VECTR or an ATT&CK Navigator layer.

Shelf: MITRE ATT&CK detection strategy pages on attack.mitre.org, SigmaHQ, Red Canary's Atomic Red Team + threat detection report, Sysdig's reverse-shell detection writeup (genuinely excellent rule engineering), FoxIO's JA4+ and ja4db.com, RITA for beacon analytics.

Want me to turn this into a chain-to-telemetry matrix for your lab — stage / technique ID / event source / example Sigma logic / emulation test — or map it against your actual pipelines and flag the blind spots?

transcript.prompt: Now the architecture: listener side, payload side, and the transport, and how they negotiate.
transcript.response:
Architecture layer, then — the whole C2 world collapses to a triangle: team server, listener, implant. Everything else (profiles, sleep masks, BOFs, redirectors) is a layer on top of that. Here's each side, then how they negotiate the session. ⚙

THE TRIANGLE
- Team server: attacker hub. Operators connect to IT (a separate channel from the implant one). Queues tasks, stores loot and config.
- Listener: the endpoint implants talk to. A protocol handler bound to a port.
- Implant: code on the target. Sleeps, wakes, polls, executes, posts results.
- Redirector: cheap VPS (nginx/apache) in front, so the real team server IP never touches targets. Disposable by design — burn it, spin another in minutes.
Key insight to hold: listener + wire profile + implant config are a MATCHED SET, compiled together. You can't mix protocols freely.

LISTENER SIDE
- Two directions: reverse (the common one — victim dials out, works through egress) and bind (implant listens; needs inbound reach to the victim). Reverse dominates for the asymmetry we covered last time.
- One listener per protocol: HTTP, HTTPS, DNS, SMB named pipe, raw TCP, mTLS, WireGuard UDP. The implant is built to match a specific listener.
- The listener is where the check-in "contract" lives: URIs, headers, encoding transforms — Cobalt Strike's malleable profiles, Sliver's C2 config. That's what defines "valid traffic" in both directions.
- Staging listeners are separate from control listeners: Sliver's stage-listener serves stage-2 payloads on specific URLs (default file extension .woff). That's a fetch endpoint, not the command channel.
- Infra-wise this is where most indicators live: default-config JA3/JA4/JA4X, cert reuse across engagements (CS's shared beacon_keys made this a clustering goldmine until Sliver's per-binary keys broke it), JARM scans of egress destinations.

PAYLOAD SIDE
- Stager vs stageless: a stager is a tiny stage-0 (often <4KB) whose only job is fetch + run stage-1 in memory; stageless embeds the whole implant in the first payload (bigger, no second fetch). Staged ops leave TWO network events (the fetch, then the callback); stageless leave one. Different detection sequences.
- Shellcode vs binary: PIC shellcode run by a loader stub vs a full executable (Sliver's raw Go binaries are ~16MB and obvious, so shellcode-into-stub is the norm). The loader/wrapper is where evasion usually lives.
- Two operational shapes, very different on the wire: beacon mode (asynchronous: sleep -> wake -> poll -> execute -> post results -> sleep) and session mode (persistent interactive socket, real-time, louder). You can promote a beacon to a session mid-op and push it back down.
- Sleep + jitter: interval ± randomized percentage. Jitter defeats "exactly every 60 seconds" signatures but clusters statistically over long windows — mean, stddev, and jitter-ratio analysis is literally how RITA-style beacon scoring works.
- Sleep obfuscation (Havoc's Ekko etc.): the implant encrypts itself in memory between callbacks. Explains why memory scanning has a timing problem, not just a capability problem.
- In-memory execution (BOFs, inline assemblies): runs inside the implant process — no child processes, so process-lineage detections go dark. Detection shifts to memory + network.
- Key material baked at compile time: either a shared keypair across implants (clusterable by defenders) or per-binary keys (not clusterable). Framework choice changes what infra correlation you can do.

TRANSPORT SIDE
- The menu and its tradeoffs: HTTP(S) blends with web traffic; mTLS is TLS with client certs (handshake doesn't look like a browser); DNS works through almost any egress control but is slow and loud; SMB named pipes chain C2 between internal hosts; WireGuard shows up as brief encrypted UDP bursts; raw TCP and ICMP/custom make up the tail.
- Fallback chains are standard: Sliver's default sequential strategy tries mTLS -> WireGuard -> HTTP(S) -> DNS, with multiple connection strings (DNS name first, bare IP as fallback when name resolution fails).
- Framing: tasks and results get wrapped per profile — metadata transforms, payloads hidden in cookies/URIs/headers, protobuf chunking for DNS. Sliver's DNS C2 even fingerprints the resolver first (CRC checks) to decide base58 vs base32 encoding per query.
- Stage transfer is often a different channel than control, compressed and encrypted "for obfuscation as much as secrecy."
- Named-pipe chaining: the internal box never egresses — its C2 rides through the edge host's pipe. Detection-side: pipe creation telemetry (Sysmon EID 17/18) and default pipe names (MSSE-*, postex_*, msagent_*, framework UUID formats).

HOW THEY NEGOTIATE (the lifecycle)
1. Execution: loader runs the implant on target; ideally stays in memory. Sloppier kits leave environment checks in plain sight.
2. Registration: implant opens the transport to its listener and presents identity + metadata (hostname, user, PID, OS, privileges). It gets a per-process ID used for the life of that process; mTLS implants present a client cert embedded at compile time.
3. Key exchange: embedded asymmetric material wraps a session key (or a per-binary keypair does); renegotiation can happen mid-session.
4. Stage fetch (if staged): pull stage-2 from the staging URL, decrypt/decompress, execute in memory, then the real callback begins.
5. Tasking loop: sleep ± jitter -> poll -> pull queued tasks -> execute -> post results. It's async: results can wait for the next cycle, and a long-running task blocks its same-cycle results.
6. Mode switch: promote beacon -> interactive session when hands-on-keyboard is needed (long-poll or persistent connection), demote back to quiet.
7. Resilience: fallback connection strings, rotating redirectors, kill dates, schedule windows.

WHAT EACH LAYER HANDS DEFENDERS
- Listener/infra: JARM scans of egress; default TLS fingerprints; cert reuse clustering; brand-new domain + TLS from a server subnet.
- Payload: injection events (Sysmon EID 8 CreateRemoteThread, EID 10), unsigned image loads (EID 7), lineage anomalies, and for staged: a process doing its first-ever network fetch.
- Transport: sessions are long-lived connections (easy); beacons need cadence statistics; DNS C2 leaks by throughput (Sliver's DNS is built for speed, not stealth — it says so); WireGuard is UDP bursts; pipes show up in 17/18.
- Negotiation: first-callback timing vs the exploit timestamp, check-in regularity over long windows, per-process destination novelty, response-size consistency per cycle.

PURPLE TEAM READS
- Emulate BOTH shapes: scheduled beacon ops and promoted interactive sessions leave different signatures. Test your detections against both.
- Staged vs stageless changes the event sequence (extra fetch + load events) — test both, assert which fires.
- Redirector test: does anything in your stack see the hop, or does only the team server side have telemetry?
- Standing gap list: beacon analytics (needs long baselines), process-level destination novelty, named-pipe telemetry, memory visibility against sleep obfuscation.

Want me to do a worked example next — one chain end-to-end (say Sliver mTLS), stage by stage, with the exact event IDs at each hop? It makes a solid lab emulation spec and feeds directly into the chain-to-telemetry matrix.

transcript.prompt: Now the transport layer: how the channel is established over TCP with no inbound listener reachable.
transcript.response:
Transport layer — and here's the key mental flip: "no inbound listener reachable" isn't an obstacle the attacker works around, it's the design. Nothing inbound ever needs to exist on the target side. What makes the channel possible is that TCP is symmetric once established: the target dials out, and everything the attacker ever sends rides back through a hole that the target's own outbound packet punched. Walk it in three moves: punch the exit, renew the lease, speak the dialect. 📡

1. PUNCH THE EXIT (the establishment, step by step)

a. connect(): the implant's process opens a socket and calls connect() to the listener endpoint. Kernel picks an ephemeral source port, sends SYN. This is an inside-out flow — it survives egress policy because it's the normal direction of corporate traffic, and it needs zero inbound rules on the target.

b. The stateful NAT: the gateway rewrites the source to its public IP and allocates a mapping port (that's PAT — many internal sockets multiplexed behind one public address). Crucially, it writes a flow-state entry for this 5-tuple. That entry IS the aperture: return traffic gets passed because it matches established state, not because anyone opened a firewall door.

c. The listener side: SYN arrives on the attacker's listening socket; accept() spawns the per-connection socket. One listening port multiplexes any number of victims — a listener is not a per-target resource, which is why "team server + one listener" scales to hundreds.

d. SYN-ACK comes back; the gateway matches its state entry, rewrites the destination back to the internal ip:port, the target's kernel completes the handshake.

e. ESTABLISHED. Now the flow is fully bidirectional. The attacker's commands travel "inbound" over a connection that was initiated outbound by the victim. The target has no listener, opened no port, and no inbound rule was ever involved. The only hole is the NAT mapping — and it's one-sided by construction.

Two details worth holding: the mapping is a lease, not a deed — every device expires idle state entries (minutes on cheap gear, up to days on Linux's conntrack defaults), and carrier-grade or enterprise NAT is just the same trick at scale. And the target-side endpoint is a client socket owned by a specific process — which is why process-to-socket attribution keeps coming up as the prime host telemetry.

2. RENEW THE LEASE (why beacons look like they do)

- The mapping dies on idle. Keepalives — or full check-in cycles — exist partly to keep it warm, exactly like SSH's ServerAliveInterval for ordinary NAT traversal. An idle implant isn't being coy; it's letting its hole close.
- Two wire shapes: session mode = one long-lived ESTABLISHED flow, heartbeats during quiet stretches. Beacon mode = connect, task, close, reconnect next cycle — every cycle is a fresh establishment with a fresh NAT entry, and a fresh detection opportunity. Persistent-flow-with-long-sleep is the hybrid.
- Reconnect logic on failure: backoff + jitter, then fallback connection strings — try mTLS, then WireGuard, then HTTP(S), then DNS; DNS name first, bare IP if resolution fails. The channel doesn't just establish once; it re-negotiates its way through whatever still works.
- TCP realities that shape all of this: half-open connections after network blips, SO_KEEPALIVE defaults that are uselessly slow (hours), so implants roll their own heartbeat. Interactive latency vs Nagle etc. — the transport is doing real engineering, not just sending bytes.

3. THE DIALECT ON TOP (roles inside the flow)

- TLS role inversion: the implant is the TLS client; the listener is the TLS server. The handshake runs inside an already-established TCP flow — the attacker plays "server" despite never being dialed inbound. Certs are self-signed or pinned; mTLS adds a client cert embedded at compile time; SNI is set to whatever the destination should look like.
- Proxied egress changes the mechanics: if the target's network only allows an egress proxy, the implant asks the proxy to dial for it — CONNECT attacker:443 (or SOCKS). The question shifts from "can I route there" to "will policy let this CONNECT through." Reachability becomes a policy question, and proxy logs become the choke point.
- Then the application layer from the last message: registration, key exchange, tasking loop.

4. WHEN EVEN THE LISTENER END ISN'T REACHABLE

- Redirector hop: the reachable endpoint is an nginx/cloud VPS that forwards to the team server. Disposable by design.
- CDN fronting: the reachable endpoint is a major CDN's edge; routing happens inside the CDN. Status in 2026: the majors clamped classic fronting back around 2018–2020, but it's per-provider — empirical studies still find plenty of smaller CDNs that route on Host regardless of SNI, and serverless edges have surfaced as new fronting paths (AWS Lambda permitting SNI/Host mismatch as of early 2026 research; Azure rejecting it). Test, don't assume. Detection: SNI-vs-Host header mismatch at the TLS-terminating point.
- No operator presence at all — store-and-forward. The implant polls a service the environment already trusts (paste sites, GitHub, cloud storage, and most documented: bot APIs like Telegram), reads tasking out of innocuous content, executes, and posts results back. No listener exists anywhere, ever. The trade: latency and throughput (it's polling, not a live pipe) and a detection problem that's purely behavioral — a non-browser process fetching a trusted platform followed within a short window by a connection to a new destination is the signal, and low-jitter polling of those platforms from hosts that have no business touching them (servers, DCs) is the hunt. This is why MITRE gave it its own technique ID (T1102.001) with detection strategies built around causal sequencing rather than indicators.
- Both-ends-NAT (botnet flavor, rare for classic C2): rendezvous service plus TCP simultaneous open — hole punching. One line, because it's mostly a p2p mesh story.

5. WHAT THE ESTABLISHMENT INSTANT LOOKS LIKE

- The invariant that shapes the whole defender strategy: flows always originate inside-out. You never "listen for inbound C2"; you watch egress and endpoints.
- The instant of establishment is a discrete, timestampable event — which is exactly what makes it detectable: first-seen destination for that process, a new external IP with TLS from a host that normally doesn't egress, and NAT/firewall logs recording a new mapping creation (the cheapest breadcrumb at scale — every establishment is logged by the device that owns the aperture).
- Lease renewal is the rhythm signature: heartbeat = tiny steady packets on an otherwise idle long flow; beaconing = periodic short flows, each with a fresh mapping; session = one long conn. Cadence analysis over long windows catches all three.
- The seam framing from message one lands here: establishment is the last moment with a hard timestamp before everything gets ciphertext-shaped. If you're building detections, anchor time correlation here — exploit -> first callback -> tasking — because downstream is only behavioral.

Offer stays open: worked example (Sliver mTLS end-to-end, exact event IDs per hop) or the chain-to-telemetry matrix — both feed a lab emulation spec, happy to build either next.

transcript.prompt: Now the shell side: how a command interpreter is attached to the socket on the target end.
transcript.response:
Shell side. The core fact that makes all of this legible: on Unix, attaching an interpreter to a socket is not a feature of the interpreter — it's three small integers being repointed. The shell never learns it's on a network; it reads fd 0 and writes fd 1/2, and those handles just happen to be a TCP connection. Everything defenders see at this layer comes from that wiring. 🐚

1. THE MECHANISM (Unix, exact sequence)

- Someone opens a TCP socket and gets an fd back. Who opens it varies: bash can do it itself (its /dev/tcp pseudo-device turns a redirection into a socket — that's the classic one-liner), a runtime can do it in-process (Python/Perl/PHP/Ruby shells), or a wrapper can exec the interpreter with the socket already open and inherited.
- The socket fd is duplicated onto 0, 1, 2 — dup2 onto stdin/stdout/stderr (dup3 and fcntl's F_DUPFD are the same move under other names). stderr is optional but usually folded in, because error text and prompts are what make the shell usable.
- The interpreter is exec'd. Unix keeps file descriptors open across execve unless FD_CLOEXEC was set — so the new process is born with its standard streams already wired to the network. For bash, -i flips it interactive; a detail that trips people up: prompts go to stderr, which is why variants that skip stderr redirection look prompt-less.
- From that instant, attacker bytes read() off fd 0 are commands, and command output write()s to fd 1. That's the whole machine. Often it's two steps: a parent shell or runtime opens the socket and spawns the child interpreter pre-wired (the bash case is literally: parent opens connection, redirects, spawns bash -i as a child).

2. THE THREE SHAPES (and their kernel-level fingerprints)

The variants aren't stylistic — they wire differently and leave different evidence:

Shape 1 — direct attach. The interpreter's own stdio IS the socket. Visible in procfs as /proc/PID/fd/0 → "socket:[inode]". Falco/Sysdig read it as proc.stdin.type in (ipv4, ipv6); Red Canary's analytic checks stdin==socket:[*] && stdout==socket:[*] on *sh processes. Cleanest signature in the business. Known noise sources: VS Code remote terminals, Cursor/Windsurf servers — tools that legitimately wire shells to sockets.

Shape 2 — relay attach. The parent owns the socket (and usually the crypto); the interpreter gets pipes — pipe() pairs or socketpair() — and the parent runs a copy loop: socket→pipe→child stdin, child stdout→pipe→socket. Python's pty.spawn is exactly this (a select() loop shuttling master↔stdout and stdin↔master). Most C2 framework "shell" commands work this way, and Windows named-pipe relays too. Footprint: shell stdio is pipe:[inode]; process-to-socket attribution lands on the parent, not the shell; the parent looks like a long-lived byte switchboard.

Shape 3 — shell-less. No interpreter at all: the implant parses commands itself, forks/execs per command, pipes output back. Shell-keyed rules get nothing to bite. Detection has to come from exec bursts with a non-shell parent plus the command sequence itself.

The lesson to bank: three shapes, three footprints. A single "hunt for reverse shells" rule catches roughly one of them — this is exactly why the category-based rule sets exist.

3. THE TTY PROJECT (why "interactive" is separate engineering)

- A socket-backed shell is functionally crippled: programs call isatty(), get false, and switch to block buffering — output arrives in chunks (the "fresh shell seems dead, then dumps everything at once" feel). No reliable prompts, no line editing, no tab completion, no job control. Ctrl+C travels as a raw 0x03 byte that usually kills the shell instead of interrupting the foreground job — because there's no line discipline left to translate it into a signal.
- The fix is a pseudo-terminal: master/slave pair (/dev/ptmx). The interpreter attaches to the slave, gets isatty()=true and real terminal semantics — line discipline, signals, the works — while the master's far end gets wired to the socket. Runtimes do it for you (pty.spawn's forkpty; socat's pty option), or you see the manual upgrade ritual: spawn a pty'd shell, background it, stty raw -echo, foreground — which is nothing more than reconciling terminal modes between the socket and the pty (raw at the local end, echo off, or you get double echo).
- Detection angle: pty allocation mid-lineage is its own event (/dev/ptmx opens, forkpty). A python3 -c running pty.spawn as a child of a network-connected shell is about as close to unambiguous as a single indicator gets — if you catch the upgrade, you're watching hands-on-keyboard in real time.

4. WINDOWS IS A DIFFERENT MECHANIC

- No fd abstraction to repoint: CreateProcess takes explicit handles. The attach is socket handle cast to HANDLE → STARTUPINFO.hStdInput/hStdOutput/hStdError + STARTF_USESTDHANDLES + bInheritHandles=TRUE → cmd.exe or powershell.exe starts with its console I/O pointed at the socket. That struct setup IS the attach — same outcome, manual wiring.
- Relay is just as common: parent keeps the socket, child gets anonymous or named pipes, parent shuttles. Named pipes can ride SMB over TCP 445 — which is why you get Sysmon EID 17 (pipe created) detections and AMSI hits on NamedPipeClientStream/ServerStream, pipe classes almost nothing benign touches.
- PowerShell shells are a third thing entirely: no attach at all. The PS process is the interpreter and the network stack in one — read loop, Invoke-Expression, write back. Footprint is script-block/AMSI shaped, not handle-shaped.

5. WHAT THE ATTACH MOMENT LEAVES

- Kernel-truth telemetry: procfs fd symlinks (socket:[...], pipe:[...]) — it doesn't depend on your log config, and eBPF/EDR sensors expose it as process-stream fields; script-level sensors can even catch the dup2-to-socket-then-spawn-shell pattern inside script content.
- Lineage plus the missing tty: a service/app process spawning an interpreter; an interpreter with no controlling terminal where humans always have one.
- Relay texture: a parent shaped like a switchboard — socket on one side, pipe pair on the other, long-lived copy loop. Attribute the socket to the parent.
- Windows: EID 17/18 pipe events, AMSI pipe-class strings, and inherited-handle lineage you have to correlate from EID 1 plus the parent's socket.
- The buffering tell: chunked, latency-feeling output is the furniture of a non-tty shell — good triage intuition when you're staring at a live session.

Full stack's now mapped: transport punched the hole, the session negotiated on top, the interpreter got wired in at the end. Natural next step if this were my lab: turn it into test cases — one emulation per shape (direct, relay, shell-less) plus the pty upgrade as its own event, and assert which telemetry fires for each. Offer still stands for that matrix or the Sliver worked example — just say the word.

WHAT payload.py DOES — three modes, one per attach shape from the stack series:
- `--mode exec` (default): connects out, dup2s the socket onto fd 0/1/2, execs the shell. Produces the flagship telemetry — a shell process with network-typed stdio.
- `--mode pty`: allocates a pty (80x24), shell on the slave, parent shuttles bytes master<->socket. Produces the pty-allocation + relay footprint.
- `--mode relay`: shell on pipes, parent shuttle. Produces the pipe-typed stdio footprint.
- On connect it sends a one-line registration banner (host / user / pid / UTC) unless `--no-banner` — emulates the check-in and gives you first-callback timing data in the listener's notes.
- Lab guard: refuses public destination addresses unless `--allow-public` (loopback / RFC1918 / link-local / Tailscale 100.64.0.0/10 pass by default). Deliberately non-evasive: no crypto, no obfuscation, no persistence, no reconnect loop — it's built to light up your sensors, not dodge them. C2-grade features are Sliver/Mythic territory, and that's the right place for them.

    PAYLOAD-OK
    ubuntu
    Linux
  Session stats: sent 40B, received 305B. Note how much telemetry-goodness falls out of that one run: the registration line, the two non-tty warnings, the prompt, and the outputs — everything a detection needs to key on, timestamped in `.log` and byte-exact in `.log.recv`.

ONE DELIBERATE OMISSION
The shell-less shape (per-command exec, no interpreter process) isn't a mode here — it's a forwarding loop rather than an attach variant, and it exists specifically to starve shell-based detections of a process to key on. That belongs in your emulation framework (Caldera / Atomic Red Team have coverage for its exec-burst-with-non-shell-parent footprint), not bolted onto a passthrough harness. transcript.prompt: Now the session handling: how the harness multiplexes, handles disconnects, and logs the transcript.
transcript.response:
Session handling done — the harness is now a proper rig: multiplexed, disconnect-aware, and transcript-backed. 🧪

WHAT CHANGED (listener.py v2, now 608 lines)

Multiplexing — thread per session, no serial bottleneck:
- Cap of `--max-sessions` (64 default); over-cap connections get rejected and logged, not silently dropped.
- Console dialect (colon commands, so bare lines stay safe for broadcast): `:sessions`, `:attach N`, `:send N TEXT`, `:kill N`, `:expect N`, `:wait [SECS]`, `:quit`.
- Bare lines go to all active sessions; in scripted runs they're also queued, and every new session receives the backlog on connect — one command batch reaches every emulated endpoint, even ones that connect late.
- `:expect N` declares the run's session count so scripted runs wait for exactly the sessions they know are coming (with a `--connect-grace` fallback when nothing is declared).

Disconnect handling — every close path tells a distinct, recorded story:
- Peer close → finalized in place: reason, byte counts, duration into `notes.log` and `index.log`, notice on console.
- `:kill N` → listener-side drop, labelled "closed by operator (:kill)".
- Shutdown → active sessions closed cleanly and labelled "closed by listener shutdown" (fixed during testing — previously everything said "peer closed"; reason tracking now distinguishes peer / operator / shutdown).
- TCP keepalives (30s/10s/3) on accepted sockets so dead peers get reaped. Payload side gained `--retry N --retry-delay S` for connect-failure reruns — each reconnect shows up as a fresh session id, which is exactly how establishment cycles look in the telemetry from the earlier messages.

Transcripts — per-session bundles under `--log DIR` (note: it's a directory now):
- `DIR/index.log` — run + session lifecycle; numbering continues across runs in the same dir.
- `DIR/session-NNNN/notes.log` — events: connect, backlog delivery, attach/detach, close + stats.
- `DIR/session-NNNN/recv.bin` / `send.bin` — raw bytes, byte-exact ground truth for evidence and sensor diffing.
- `DIR/session-NNNN/transcript.log` — readable merged view.

transcript.prompt: Now the encoding layer: how the payload is staged and encoded for delivery in a lab, and how the target decodes it.
transcript.response:
Delivery layer done — staged, encoded, and decode chains all executable now, with receipts. 📦

WHAT SHIPPED — `delivery.py` (three moves) + `tests/delivery_smoke.sh`

- `serve` — single-file stage server with request logging: timestamp, client, user-agent, status, bytes — including misses (404s logged too, which is its own detection nuance). That log is the "web server side" view of a stage fetch.
- `stager` — prints the fetch-and-run line for a stage URL (`curl` / `wget` / `ps` styles).
- `encode` — packages a file as an encoded one-liner with its decode chain: `b64`, `hex`, `gzip-b64`, `ps-b64` (UTF-16LE base64 for `-EncodedCommand`), plus `--blob-only` for scripting.

THE THREE SHAPES AND THEIR TELEMETRY COST (the design frame, now in the README):
- staged: stager fetches the real payload, then runs it → TWO network events — the fetch, then the callback. The stage log and the session transcript timestamp both — that gap is the sequence your correlation rules live on.
- encoded: payload rides inline as a text blob → one network event, but the decode chain lands in process telemetry (`sh → echo → base64 -d → gunzip → bash`), and the blob itself is a command-line anchor.
- stageless: what payload.py does today — one event, nothing else.

One deliberate scope line, stated in the tool: transport-grade encodings only. Base64/hex/gzip/`-EncodedCommand` are *legible* formats — they exist so your detections have something to catch. No crypters, no AMSI/ETW tricks, no encryption-for-evasion; if it's in this kit, it's supposed to light up your sensors.

VERIFICATION
- `delivery_smoke.sh`: 5/5 —

  - ps-b64 structural check: blob → base64 → UTF-16LE → byte-identical source.
  - full staged chain: stage server + stager fetch + payload + listener session, with both log ends asserted:

      transcript marker: `ubuntu@vps-6f81eb95:~/purple-lab$ echo STAGED-OK; exit`

- Encoded full chain, live: `encode --format gzip-b64` produced a 175-char one-liner; executed it as a target would (`echo '<blob>' | base64 -d | gunzip | bash`); it decoded, ran payload.py, connected back, and the session served cleanly — transcript shows the banner, both bash warnings, prompt, `ENCODED-OK`, `exit`. Chain exit 0.
- One environment catch: this box already has services on 8090/8099, so the serve default was moved to 8842 (verified free) before anything collided.

transcript.prompt: I work in security awareness. Give me the landscape: what does the modern phishing-simulation industry actually deliver to enterprise customers, and how does it differ from real phishing?
transcript.response:
🎣 Phishing-simulation landscape, Sep 2026: what enterprises actually buy, and where sims ≠ real phishing.

WHAT CUSTOMERS ACTUALLY GET
- Simulation engine: large lure-template libraries, difficulty tiers, scheduling + randomization, group targeting (new hires, finance, execs), localization. Channels expanding past email: smishing, vishing, collaboration-app lures.[6]
- Capture + telemetry: fake M365 / Okta / DocuSign / VPN login pages; logs click, data-submit, report; just-in-time "you clicked" teaching pages.
- Reporting loop: Outlook/Gmail report buttons (PAB-style) + triage platforms (PhishER, Cofense Triage) wired into SOC workflows.
- Training + compliance: micro-learning, gamified modules, auto-enrollment on fail; mapped to HIPAA, PCI DSS, SOC 2, CMMC; audit-ready evidence trails.[5]
- Analytics: PPP, report rate, industry benchmarks, exec dashboards — marketed now as "human risk management": per-user risk scoring, adaptive tracks, AI-generated lures.[4]
- Market: security awareness training ≈ USD 5.77B (2025) → USD 6.74B (2026), 16.82% CAGR to USD 14.66B (2031); leaders KnowBe4, Proofpoint, Cofense, Hoxhunt, SoSafe; sim vendors buying email security (KnowBe4 + Egress) to pitch end-to-end human-path testing.[4][5]
- Real buying drivers: audits + cyber insurance — quarterly sim metrics increasingly required, premium discounts cited up to 20%.[4]

WHERE SIMS DIVERGE FROM REAL PHISHING
1. Sims bypass your defenses by design. Standard deployment whitelists sim mail (IP, header, or SPF) and carves SEG exceptions — Cisco's own doc walks through skipping spam, virus, and AMP engines for sim traffic.[7][8] Sims therefore don't measure whether email defenses would stop anything; they measure the human only, under conditions defenders engineered.
2. Metric corruption when bypass is sloppy: without Safe Links / Safe Attachments exceptions, filters pre-click links and pre-open attachments — fake clicks, fake opens, inflated numbers.[7]
3. Finish line = click or form submit. Real campaigns: AiTM proxies (Evilginx-class) stealing session tokens, OAuth consent phishing, QR-code lures.[13] Real scale: human element in 62% of breaches, social engineering = 16% of breaches, phishing flat at 16% of initial access; FBI IC3's latest report: 191,561 phishing complaints, USD 3.05B BEC losses.[14][15]
4. Content realism gap: templates + merge fields vs OSINT-built, event-timed (payroll, M&A, tax season), adaptive, multi-stage (email-bomb → phone call → AiTM). DBIR 2026: mobile-centric attacks (text, voice) land ~40% higher median click rates than email — while most sim programs are still email-only.[14]
5. Recognition ≠ vigilance: staff learn simulator signatures (vendor domains, headers, recurring templates). NIST Phish Scale data from a 12.5k-employee reproduction: lure difficulty moves click rates from 7.0% (easy) to 15.0% (hard) — more than any training did; orgs hitting 2% click targets may just be using easy lures.[9]
6. Independent evidence on training is weak: same 12.5k study — no significant training effect on click (p=0.450) or report (p=0.417) rates[9]; 19.5k-employee, 8-month healthcare RCT — near-zero absolute effect, static training possibly counterproductive, interactive training ~19% better only for full completers[10]. Long-term IEEE S&P 2022 work saw embedded training backfire, though employee crowd-reporting worked as a detection layer[11]; scoping review of 42 studies — ~23% remain susceptible, sustained-change evidence limited; active, repeated, feedback-rich practice outperforms annual sessions[12].

READING THE NUMBERS
KnowBe4 2026 benchmark: baseline PPP 33.2% → 20.1% at 90 days → 4.2% at 12 months; worst industries Healthcare & Pharma (42.7%), Insurance (38.1%); larger orgs worse (24.7% under 250 staff vs 39.5% at 10,000+).[1][2][3] That's measured on the vendor's own sims — usually allowlisted, often recognizable. Independent RCTs under realistic conditions find ~no significant training effect on click/report rates, with lure difficulty dominating outcomes.[9][10] Both can be true at once. PPP is recognition of vendor sims. It is not attack immunity. (PPP itself counts clicks, opens, or "engagement" per vendor definition — read the fine print.)[2]

WHAT SIMS ARE GENUINELY GOOD FOR
- 🛡️ Reporting-habit muscle + exercising the triage/SOC pipeline at scale — crowd-sourced detection is the demonstrated win.[11]
- Trendable susceptibility signal — when lure difficulty is held constant and reported.
- Compliance + insurance evidence and exec-friendly dashboards.[4]
- Safe rehearsal of new channels (smish, vish) with no operational risk.[6]

DIRECTION OF TRAVEL (2026)
- "Human risk management" everywhere: risk scoring, gamification and positive reinforcement; AI orchestration ships this year — KnowBe4 AIDA Orchestration (Feb 2026), Cofense AI campaign detection + assistant (May 2026); Hoxhunt reports 14x growth in AI-generated phishing.[5]
- Budget tension: auditors and insurers want quarterly sim evidence while 36% of CISOs report cutting training funds to feed XDR stacks.[4]
- Mature programs: phishing-resistant MFA + DMARC first — that kills most of the AiTM/OAuth playbook regardless of training[13] — then sims as behavior telemetry: track report rate and time-to-report, not just PPP; pair with social-engineering red-team exercises; compare sim catch rates against real-inbox catch rates.

BOTTOM LINE: sims are a safe, scalable instrument for susceptibility signal, reporting habit, and compliance evidence. They are not threat coverage, not a defense-stack test, not a predictor of real-attack behavior. Judge vendors on what they measure, which channels they cover, and whether their traffic is allowlisted.

transcript.prompt: Now the campaign architecture — how a platform models a campaign from audience to reporting.
transcript.response:
🎯 Campaign architecture — how a platform models a campaign, audience → reporting.

PIPELINE
directory sync → users → segments (static | smart rules) → campaign (content × delivery × schedule) → per-recipient events → response → aggregates → reports
└──────────────────── smart-group rules re-feed the next campaign ────────────────────┘

1) AUDIENCE + SEGMENTS
- Audience is a controlled directory: users are imported/synced first, then provisioned, updated, and de-provisioned automatically from the org directory (Cofense "Recipient Sync"; KnowBe4 import-first requirement).[3][8]
- Two group species: static uploaded groups, and dynamic "smart" groups — pure rules, auto add/remove, refreshed every 15 minutes (time-window rules refresh once daily ~06:00 UTC).[5]
- The rule language spans: user fields (title, location, custom fields), user dates, phishing events (delivered / failed / reported with counts + windows like "failed > 0 in the last 4 weeks"), training state, assessment scores, external events via API. Up to 5 criteria per group, all must match (multiple values inside one criterion OR together).[5][6]
- Hygiene is built into the model: only active users enrol, archived users excluded; inactive accounts skew PPP, so exclusion groups are standard practice — plus audit groups that verify the automation actually fired.[5][6]

2) THE CAMPAIGN OBJECT
- A campaign is nothing but a composition of referenced assets + settings. GoPhish is the canonical open-source shape: build sending profile → import groups → template → landing page → launch; the campaign binds them with a launch / send-by window.[1][2]
- Commercial wizard matches: name; send-to (all users or specific groups); template topic, specific template, language override; difficulty rating (1–5 stars); phish link domain (random by default); frequency; start time; sending period; track-activity window; track-replies toggle; "add clickers to" remediation group; admin report toggle.[3][6][7]
- Personalization at send time: per-recipient merge fields + a unique tracking URL injected into each copy; link-domain rotation avoids pattern recognition.[1][6]
- Vector menu: link, attachment, data-entry, spear, reply-to, QR — plus difficulty tiers to dial realism per audience.[4][6]
- Scenario sourcing is its own layer: Cofense feeds sims from live threat intel — including phish that actually bypassed SEGs ("SEG Misses" filter) — so the simulator mirrors what lands in real inboxes.[8]
- Lifecycle: created → scheduled → running → completed; the results view is the campaign's home screen.[1]

3) SCHEDULING + DELIVERY
- Start time defaults to business hours; "sending period" chooses burst vs trickle — all at once, or spread over e.g. 6 business days / 3 weeks; the track-activity window (e.g. 6 days after last email) freezes when stats are computed.[6][7]
- Frequency ladder: one-time, weekly, bi-weekly, monthly, quarterly.[7][17]
- Field guidance: monthly baseline for everyone, bi-weekly for finance/IT/execs; new hires simulated within their first weeks; 20–30 distinct scenarios needed before results mean anything.[13][14]
- "Responsive delivery" abandons fixed clock times and sends when the recipient is active in their inbox — kills timezone and Friday-16:00 artifacts.[8]

4) EVENTS — WHAT GETS RECORDED
- Per-recipient state machine: sent → opened (pixel) → clicked (redirect) → submitted data (landing page) → reported (button) → replied (optional). Every hop appends to a raw event stream; timeline view per recipient; device/OS/browser parsed from user-agent; IP + geo captured.[1][4]
- Counting semantics are defined, not implied: one simulated phish can yield multiple failures — click + data entry = two failures but one failed test; personal PPP counts failures, not tests.[5]
- If credential capture is enabled on a landing page, the platform records and displays the typed values — a deliberate configuration choice with data-handling implications.[1]

5) RESPONSE LOOP
- Fail → just-in-time education page → auto-group assignment ("add clickers to") → remedial training that escalates: 1st fail → round 1, exactly 2 fails → round 2, 3+ fails → round 3; audit groups prove the enrollments happened.[3][6]
- Report → first-class citizen: the reporting button (PAB etc.) feeds both the metrics and the reporting/triage pipeline.[4]
- Positive reinforcement is part of the loop — stars, streaks, leaderboards reward reporting, not just punish clicking.[16]

6) REPORTING LAYER
- Aggregates derive from the event log: campaign summary = PPP, click rate, data-entry rate, report rate, time-to-report, repeat offenders — sliceable by group; admin email report fires after the tracking window; CSV export covers results + raw events.[1][3][7]
- Vendor-superset scores sit on top: Cofense "resilience" = report-only users ÷ users who fell; >1.0 means the org detects more than it loses; report rate = leading indicator, click rate = lagging.[9][10]
- Field targets: report rate should exceed click rate in a mature program; median time-to-report under 30 min at the top end; track P50/P75/P90 because the distribution is bimodal — first wave <1h, second wave 3–8h, and reporting friction adds ~8–12 min per report.[11][12]

7) 🔁 THE FEEDBACK ENGINE — WHERE "CAMPAIGN" BECOMES SYSTEM
- Results re-enter as rules, not dashboards: smart groups refresh (15 min) and tier users by failures; fail → dropped to an easier difficulty band, two consecutive passes → promoted back; each tier runs as its own recurring campaign with its own cadence and star band.[6]
- Newer engines skip fixed campaigns entirely: pick the simulation per employee per cycle from skill/role/org-chart/live threat intel, ~10-day cadence, tighter for repeat clickers, across email/SMS/voice/Teams/deepfake. Case color: 963 unique variants across 202,992 sims, reporting 24% → 50%+.[15][16]

8) IF YOU'RE MODELLING IT YOURSELF
- Entities: user, group (static | rule), template, landing page, sending profile, campaign, enrollment (frozen roster snapshot at launch), event, aggregate — everything else is a view. Append-only events → derived summaries; unique token per recipient for idempotent tracking; scheduler with rate limits, timezone windows, jitter; exclusions/cooldown lists; permissions + dual control on send; API/webhooks out to HRIS, triage, SIEM, insurers.[1]

BOTTOM LINE: campaign = composition (audience × content × delivery × schedule) over a frozen roster; reporting = derived aggregates over an immutable event log; the loop closes through rule-based groups re-targeting the next cycle. Measurement apparatus for human behavior. Not a defense test — sims stay allowlisted by design.

Want the full pipeline diagram as an SVG one-pager? Say the word.

transcript.prompt: Now the landing-page layer: what a simulation landing page actually is, conceptually, and what makes it convincing.
transcript.response:
🪤 The landing-page layer — what a simulation landing page actually is, and what makes it convincing.

1) WHAT IT IS
- GoPhish defines it exactly: the actual HTML pages returned to users when they click the phishing links. Post-click half of the sim — email is the lure, the landing page is the ask (credentials, data); in KnowBe4's framing it's what the user sees "if they fail a phishing test".[1][4]
- Three jobs: measure (a click is a shallow signal; the page turns it into depth — a lab study found 93% of users who clicked went on to provide their info)[9]; teach (the page IS the training channel — embedded training shown after the fall beats emailed lessons on retention and transfer)[9]; contain (resolve the visit: education page, or redirect, classically back to the genuine site "to prevent users from becoming suspicious")[1].
- Object model: a reusable asset — capture_credentials / capture_passwords flags, redirect_url, language, Ready/Draft status — attached to a campaign or inherited (KnowBe4 precedence: campaign override > per-template > account default).[2][3][5]
- Vendor models differ slightly. KnowBe4: system vs custom landing pages, WYSIWYG editor, chosen per campaign[4]; Microsoft: "landing page" (post-open page; Global built-ins vs Tenant customs with rich-text + HTML modes and merge tags like ${firstName}/${emailAddress}/${department}).[5][6]
- Separately, Microsoft models a "login page" — the credential form itself, bound to Credential Harvest / Link-in-Attachment payloads, one-page or two-page (Next → submit / "compromise" button).[6][7]
- Mechanics: per-recipient rid token → the right page renders for the right person, and without it pages aren't browsable (GoPhish throws a 404); "Import Site from URL" clones a real page into the editor; imported form data can be tagged with its original URL for later replay in red-team validation flows.[1][2]
- Safety switches define the layer: password capture is its own flag (default off in GoPhish; anything captured is stored plaintext); Microsoft states the product saves no credentials; HTML guidance says avoid name=password in custom code so values never travel as plaintext in your own plumbing. Some programs skip the page entirely (click-only sims) to isolate the email decision.[2][6][7]

2) 🎭 WHAT MAKES ONE CONVINCING — the fidelity stack
- Content fidelity carries the most weight. The classic study: 23% of participants never looked at the URL bar, status bar, or security indicators at all; padlock knowledge was near-mythical; the best-built fake fooled ~90%.[8] Users judge by page content — branding, layout, professionalism — essentially never by browser chrome. Budget goes to content: correct logo, typography, layout, local language, and the exact portal the org actually uses. The realistic target is the branded federated sign-in (company-styled SSO portal), not a generic vendor screen, because that's the experience employees already trust.[8][10]
- Context alignment: the page must complete the sentence the email started (shared doc → sign-in that makes sense; expired password → password page). Pretext-page mismatch is the classic tell.[10]
- Interaction realism: forms accept any input and advance; multi-step flows (two-page logins, Next → submit); error and confirmation states; device/OS-aware rendering — modern kits adapt the fake window per platform. Nothing may break the frame (refresh, back button, mobile layout).[6][13]
- The URL/domain layer — the deliberate tell: sims serve from domains picked to look plausible, rotating through a random pool; trained users hover, most never do. Adversaries escalate here: typosquats, homoglyphs, brand-in-subdomain tricks, aged domains, Cloudflare + valid TLS.[10] And the frontier skips the problem entirely: AiTM proxies serve the genuine page through attacker infrastructure[11]; BITB renders fake window chrome whose fake URL bar shows the real domain[13]. Device-code flows march users to Microsoft's actual login page[14]; at least one kit pulls each tenant's live branding from Microsoft's own endpoint[12].
- The security ceiling (what sims deliberately never do): relay/proxy chains, live tenant branding, session-token capture, anti-analysis (CAPTCHA gates, obfuscation, dev-tools detection, burn-and-replace domains).[11][12][13]
- Sims are staged snapshots: inert, tokenized, one brand per page, no backend relay, no real theft.[1][2]

3) HOW IT PLUGS BACK INTO THE SYSTEM
- Submit → failure accounting (click + data entry = two failures, one failed test), data-entry rate, personal PPP, smart-group rules; the education page feeds remediation; a silent redirect ends the visit cleanly.[1][4]
- Design tension program owners manage at this layer: realism vs ethics/data risk (works councils and capture policy live here), and "too obvious" sims just float confidence on template recognition.[9]

BOTTOM LINE: the landing page is the sim's ask and its classroom — convincingness is content + context + interaction fidelity, with URL/domain as the checkpoint most humans skip. The ceiling is deliberate: staged, inert, allowlisted snapshots, while real kits moved on to serving the genuine article through proxies and fake chrome.

transcript.prompt: Now the tracking layer: what gets recorded on a submit event and how it reaches the platform.
transcript.response:
📡 The tracking layer — what a submit event records, and how it reaches the platform.

1) WHAT A SUBMIT EVENT IS
- Trigger: the landing page's form POST — an ordinary HTTPS request into the sim infrastructure, scoped to the recipient by the rid token.[1][4]
- The canonical record (GoPhish, the readable specimen): {email, time, message: "Submitted Data", details}. Details carries the rid, the source address and user-agent, plus every form field submitted — each form element its own key and list of values.[1]
- Recipient-level state: id, status, ip, latitude, longitude, send_date, reported flag, modified_date; the campaign stats object rolls up total / sent / opened / clicked / submitted_data / email_reported / error.[2]
- Commercial equivalents: KnowBe4 timestamps every action — Delivered, Opened, Clicked, QR Code Scanned, Replied, Attachment Opened, Macro Enabled, Data Entered, Reported, Bounced — with browser, OS, and IP in the click drill-down.[6][7]
- Semantics of "submit": it's the depth signal. Microsoft labels outcomes per technique — credential harvest = "the user entered their credentials on the sign-in page (credentials aren't stored by Microsoft)"; OAuth-consent sim = clicked + accepted permissions; drive-by URL = the click alone is already the compromise.[10]

2) HOW IT REACHES THE PLATFORM
- The platform is a passive HTTP log collector. GoPhish says it plainly: any hit on the recipient's URL saves Time + connecting IP + User-Agent — "gophish just 'dumbly' saves them".[3]
- Attribution: at launch each recipient gets a unique rid URL; the stored mapping is URL → landing page + campaign + recipient — that's how one hit is tied to one human.[4][5]
- Path a — open: a transparent tracking pixel with a per-recipient reference; "when the image loads, we are able to track the open in our system" — and the pixel can be disabled account-wide.[6]
- Path b — click: the rid URL hit is recorded, then the visitor is redirected to the landing page.[5]
- Path c — submit: the form POST; field values serialize into the event's details payload.[1]
- Path d — report: a different channel. The add-in (PAB, Cofense Reporter) ships the reported message to the platform's API over TLS — KnowBe4: "the external IP address, user agent, and other standard browser information are sent to us as part of the standard HTTPS communication"; server-side checks classify it: valid Campaign Recipient ID header + first report within an hour + same account (PAB), and Cofense Reporter "automatically discerns emails reported from Cofense PhishMe scenarios" from real ones; sims get "automatically tabulated into exercise results", real reports land with the SOC, full headers intact.[8][17]
- Native-mailbox sensors (when the platform owns the mailbox): Microsoft harvests Read / Deleted / Forwarded / Replied / Out-of-office signals from Outlook activity — client telemetry rather than HTTP — and builds per-user action timelines from it.[12]
- Reachability is a prerequisite: if the recipient can't reach the sim server, the platform records nothing; and recording generally starts a few minutes after launch.[5][11]
- Consumption side: webhooks push the same event JSON out to an endpoint you control — optionally HMAC-SHA256-signed via an X-Gophish-Signature header — plus CSV exports and APIs (Microsoft exposes AttackSimulation.Read.All on Graph).[1][11]

3) INGESTION SEMANTICS
- Events are append-only; one recipient can generate multiples — the false-positive thread shows repeated "Clicked Link" rows for a single rid. Aggregates apply unique/first conventions over that raw log.[3]
- Counting windows freeze: KnowBe4's campaign end = first email date + sending duration + tracking duration; Microsoft captures interaction signals until the simulation ends, training events until the training due date.[6][11]
- Late reports of a closed campaign show the success message but don't register as reported in results.[8]

4) 🤖 THE NOISE FLOOR
- Scanner detonation: Microsoft's own FAQ — "Safe Links detonations are identified as clicks by the user"; URL sandboxes open links at delivery time in an isolated environment, but your tracking server takes the hit all the same.[11][15]
- Microsoft states it outright: the per-user URL is what enables attribution — "Non-Microsoft filtering services or email forwarding can lead to false positives".[10]
- Add-ins, AV, link previews, and MDM security software manufacture more hits recorded under a person's name.[9]
- Platforms fight back: honeypot links hidden in sim emails (invisible to humans, crawlable by scanners) plus timing/actor/user-agent scoring; SoSafe measures ~8% of clicks as bot-generated on average, above 15% at orgs with aggressive link scanners.[13]
- KnowBe4's bot-click heuristics: Delivered/Open/Click timestamps within a minute of each other, browsers or OS versions not present in the estate, IPs belonging to security vendors.[9]
- Opens are the weakest signal of all: Apple Mail Privacy Protection prefetches pixels through Apple's proxies at delivery — "no reliable way to distinguish a proxy prefetch from a genuine open".[16] Blocked images do the opposite — real reads never get recorded.[14] Opens confirm delivery at best.
- The practical trust tier: report / data entry / reply / click >> open — "a false positive is a statistic generated by software and recorded under a user's name".[14]

BOTTOM LINE: a submit event is an HTTPS form POST carrying rid + submitted fields + IP/user-agent/timestamp, appended as an event row keyed to recipient + campaign, rolled into stats, then shipped out via webhook / API / CSV. The platform runs no code on user machines — it only sees the callbacks its own pixels, links, and forms provoke, plus what the mail client and the report button volunteer.

Now the templating system these platforms use — how a campaign author parameterises a page: brand tokens, field sets, copy slots.
transcript.response:
🧩 Templating layer — how a campaign author parameterises a page: brand tokens, field sets, copy slots.

1) THE PARAMETER SURFACE — five token families
- Identity merge fields: per-recipient values pulled from the user directory — [[first_name]], [[last_name]], [[display_name]], [[manager_name]][4] — GoPhish's {{.FirstName}} / {{.Email}} equivalents work the same way[1].
- Infrastructure / tracking tokens: the platform-owned mechanics — {{.RId}} (unique target id), {{.URL}} (phishing URL), {{.TrackingURL}} + {{.Tracker}} (open pixel), {{.BaseURL}} (rid-stripped base for static assets)[1]; a click on the platform's own link token is what "records the simulation as failed"[11].
- Brand tokens: the org skin — [[company_name]], [[company_logo_img]] / [[company_logo_url]], [[brand_color]], [[email_banner]], [[signature]], and [[domain]] with its spoof-or-not setting[5].
- Copy slots: headline / subhead / CTA / footer strings — and they cross artifacts: landing pages can echo the email's {SUBJECT}, {FROMNAME}, {FROMEMAIL}[13] or ${FromName} / ${EmailSubject}[8]; utility tokens sprinkle dates and random digits ([[current_date_10]], [[random_number_3]])[3].
- Field sets: which inputs the page renders and what prefills them — dynamic tags can drop ${userName} into the email field[9]; capture semantics follow the field names (recognized username/password names → clean pair, anything else → raw dump)[10].

2) HOW RENDERING WORKS
- Same idea, different syntax per vendor: GoPhish {{.RId}}[1]; KnowBe4 [[first_name]][4]; Check Point {link}[11].
- FortiPhish adds filters ({{date|layout}}, {{num|min|max}})[12]; Microsoft uses ${emailAddress}[8].
- Placeholders resolve server-side at send/click time[11]; GoPhish's set is case-sensitive[1].
- Authoring UX: rich-text + HTML tabs, placeholder pickers, "Send Me a Test Email" to validate[3]; library browsing with preview and clone[6].
- Localization is a per-user parameter: templates carry language variants, campaigns can override the profile language[7]; Microsoft ships page sets in 12+ languages[8].
- The library is metadata-driven: topic, language, difficulty, updated, origin — the filters an author picks by[6]; Proofpoint surfaces each template's average customer failure rate so difficulty is visible before the send[14].

3) THE BRAND-TOKEN REALITY CHECK
- What platforms actually ship: your-org tokens (logo, brand color, name, domain)[5], curated third-party skins (Microsoft built-ins cover Microsoft, LinkedIn, GitHub, plus non-branded)[9], and AI presets that assemble a look (Microsoft 365 sign-in, Google Workspace login, Corporate VPN portal, Minimal & modern, "match a specific brand")[10].
- So a "brand token" today is a preset object + your org constants — not a design system.

4) WORKED EXAMPLE — parameterising our neutral-signin page
- The page is just render(template, context). A context covering every family:
```json
{
  "infra":     { "rid": "VYrDwtG", "url": "https://sim.example.com/?rid=VYrDwtG", "tracking_url": "https://sim.example.com/track?rid=VYrDwtG" },
  "recipient": { "email": "j.doe@corp.com", "first_name": "Jane", "department": "Finance" },
  "brand":     { "portal_name": "Corporate Portal", "logo": null, "accent": "#2563eb" },
  "copy":      { "headline": "Sign in", "subhead": "Use your account to continue.", "cta": "Sign in", "footer": "" },
  "fields":    [ { "name": "email", "type": "email", "label": "Email address", "prefill": "recipient.email" },
                 { "name": "password", "type": "password", "label": "Password" } ],
  "flow":      { "on_success": "inline", "education": "standard", "redirect": "" }
}
```
- Substitution sketch (the mental model — real platforms render server-side):
```js
const render = (tpl, ctx) => tpl.replace(/\{\{\s*([\w.]+)\s*\}\}/g, (_, key) => {
  const v = key.split('.').reduce((o, part) => (o || {})[part], ctx);
  return v == null ? '' : String(v);        // missing token → empty string
});
```
- Mapping for our template: copy slots → <h1> / .sub / button / footer; brand tokens → accent color, title, logo slot, favicon; field set → the inputs + name attributes (the capture contract); infra → the rid URL the page is served under; flow → inline reveal vs redirect.

5) ⚠️ GOTCHAS
- Raw link = dead attribution: use the link token so the per-recipient URL + rid generate, and keep the sim server reachable or the events never record[2].
- Blank in, blank out: a placeholder renders empty when the profile field is empty — fix ingestion before blaming the template[4].
- Syntax is exact and case-sensitive per platform; test-send before a live campaign[1][3].
- Field names ARE the capture contract — recognized names pair cleanly, unknown names dump raw[10]; align password-field naming with capture policy[8].
- Brand tokens are the impersonation budget: [[domain]]'s spoof toggle, org skins vs third-party presets — set policy before picking the preset[5].

BOTTOM LINE: a sim page is a function — render(template, context) — over five parameter families (identity, infra, brand, copy, fields); vendors supply the libraries (brand presets, copy templates, difficulty metadata), the author supplies the campaign's context, the field set you declare is the capture contract, and the link token you forget is the event you lose.

transcript.prompt: Now the lure layer: how a campaign notification email is composed and sent, and the CTA structure.
transcript.response:
📨 The lure layer — how the notification email is composed, sent, and how the CTA is structured.

1) THE EMAIL OBJECT
- GoPhish's definition: a template is "the content of the emails that are sent to targets" — imported from an existing email or built from scratch, with attachments and tracking images supported[1]; the API shape is name / subject / text / html / attachments (base64 content, type, name)[3].
- Microsoft frames the payload as "the link, QR code, or attachment in the simulated phishing email message that's presented to users" — the CTA is literally a first-class object[6].
- Wizard fields (MS): sender (From name, including a "use first name as display name" option; an internal From email address is explicitly called out as increasing susceptibility), subject (with an optional "External tag"), attachment name/type (Docx or HTML), phishing URL selection from a vetted list, theme/brand/industry/current-event tags, language, and a QR-code inserter with 50/100/150 px sizing[6].
- Provenance paths: library clone, custom build, or import — GoPhish imports raw emails from the client's "View Original" content ("pixel-perfect" repurposing of legitimate mail)[1][3]; Microsoft can harvest real phishing attacks reported by users into custom payloads[8].

2) HOW IT'S SENT
- A sending profile is an SMTP relay config: host:port, from_address (display name + address), optional auth, cert-error handling, custom headers[4]; nuance: the SMTP From and the visible sender header can diverge depending on provider — make the envelope match what you want users to see[5].
- Per-recipient rendering happens at send: merge tokens, the unique {{.URL}}, the {{.Tracker}} pixel[3]; attachments are parameterized too — Office docs accept template variables, a linked-image {{.TrackingURL}} records document-open, macro code hitting {{.URL}} records macro-enabled[2].
- Mass CTA rewiring is a platform feature: Microsoft's "replace all links in the email message with the phishing link" toggle, and GoPhish import's convert_links turns every link into {{.URL}}[3][6] — how a copied real email becomes a simulation without leaving live links.
- Delivery knobs: randomize send times (stagger over a 12-hour window) and region-aware delivery by the recipient's timezone setting[7]; plus the pacing/allowlist reality from earlier layers.

3) 🪝 THE CTA STRUCTURE
- Vehicle menu: hyperlink, styled button, image, attachment (open / enable content), QR code, or reply — MS payloads are link, QR, or attachment[6]; KnowBe4's vector set adds data-entry, spear, reply-to, and QR[14].
- Presentation is a measured variable: masked CTAs (button or hypertext) pull more clicks than a raw URL (χ²=34.8, p<.001, small-to-moderate effect); mobile compounds it (tap-and-hold vs hover to inspect); and rendering is client-dependent — Outlook desktop flattens a button-in-anchor to plain hypertext[9].
- The ask taxonomy, from a phishing corpus coding study: action = click 86%, download 13%; popular phrasings cluster on "verify account", "update account", "get files"[10].
- CTA → event mapping is 1:1 with the tracking layer: Clicked / Attachment Opened / Macro Enabled / QR Scanned / Replied are distinct logged events[13].
- What reaches inboxes: URL-based lures reach users about 4× more than attachments[11]. Objectives differ — links lean toward credential capture / account takeover, attachments toward execution / malware, with regular overlap[12].
- The chain rule from earlier layers still applies: CTA text and the landing page must tell one story; the MS theme enum (Invoice, Voicemail, Payroll, Password, Quarantine, …) is the canonical pretext shelf both sides draw from[6].

4) AUTHORING NOTES
- Never leave raw links: replace or convert so every CTA element carries the rid token[3][6].
- Validate URL availability before launch — Safe Browsing blocks are a real failure mode — and test-send first[1][6].
- Attachment hygiene: supported types include Office, .html, .txt, and .ics calendar invites; keep the tracker out of the email body when it's used inside the document[2].
- Keep the metadata honest: theme / brand / complexity and predicted compromise rate are what the program layer programs against later[6][7].

BOTTOM LINE: a lure is composed content (subject, sender, body, attachments) + one vehicle (link, QR, attachment, reply) + one ask; the send layer parameterizes everything per recipient and paces it; CTA presentation (masked vs raw) is measurable; and whichever CTA element gets engaged is exactly the event the tracking layer records.

transcript.prompt: Now the delivery layer: how a platform serves the page and the post-submit redirect flow.
transcript.response:
🌐 The delivery layer — how the platform serves the page and what runs after submit.

1) SERVE PATH — FROM CLICK TO RENDERED PAGE
- A landing page is "the actual HTML pages that are returned to users when they click the phishing links"[1]; the platform stores the HTML and, on request, uses the per-recipient rid "to dynamically load the correct landing page"[1].
- Browsing the listener without an rid returns a generic 404 — a live page has no public URL[1]; the serve path is scoped per-recipient from the first request.
- Operationally the server must be reachable by recipients and match its own scheme (an HTTPS phish_server needs https:// in campaign URLs); the classic self-test is "browse the URL, expect a 404 and a log line"[2].
- Domain choice is a serving parameter: platform default domain or one of your verified custom domains[3]; static assets ride the same server via its static path[1].
- Rendering is templated at serve time — gophish landing pages "support templating"[1]; Microsoft's pages substitute dynamic tags on load, including payload context (${FromName}, ${EmailSubject}, ${EmailContent})[5].

2) THE FORM AT SERVE TIME — CAPTURE SWITCHES SHAPE THE HTML
- Capture settings change what the server renders: with capture off, gophish "will remove the name attributes from your inputs so they aren't submitted with the form"[2]; capture-submitted-data and capture-passwords are separate switches, and captured credentials are stored in plaintext[1].
- The modern posture inverts the default: an OpenAEV capture-disabled page records the submission "only counted as an event"[3]; KnowBe4's system sensitive-info pages "intentionally filter out" entered data and log only that the user failed the data-entry portion[10].
- Submission wiring: OpenAEV intercepts the submit of the data-phishing-form element and posts to its tracking endpoint[3]; gophish's canonical pattern is a native form posting action="" back to the served page[2].

3) 🔀 POST-SUBMIT: THREE DOCUMENTED PATTERNS
- (a) Off-page redirect (the red-team style): gophish's "Redirect To:" exists because "to prevent users from becoming suspicious after entering credentials, you may want to redirect them to the original URL"; it needs a full URL with scheme[1]. OpenAEV exposes the same field — "where the recipient is sent after submitting the form. Leave empty to keep them on the page"[3].
- (b) Education reveal (the program style): in Microsoft, a completed sign-in attempt lands on a page that "indicates you were just phished by your security team," with identification tips and a "Go to training" link[7]; failing the simulation also triggers a training-notification email the moment they fail[8].
- (c) Wire-it-yourself: a KnowBe4 data-entry page runs select-link → data-entry form, and submitting on it counts as a phishing failure[9]. The user who submits then sees a "secondary or final landing page"[11], wired by replacing the form's action URL with the final page's URL, updated for every form tag[11].
- Which page wins is a policy layer: KnowBe4 resolves most-specific-first — template-level, then campaign-level, then the account default ("Basic 'Oops!' Landing Page")[12]. Microsoft picks landing page and login page per payload, and login pages come one-page or two-page (Page 1 "Next" → Page 2 submit) to mirror modern sign-in UX[4].
- One more variant: for drive-by URLs, Microsoft can show an interstitial overlay before the landing page — or go straight through[6].

BOTTOM LINE: the delivery layer is an rid-scoped render pipeline — the request resolves to one recipient's page, capture switches decide what the HTML even carries, and the post-submit branch is a config choice (redirect away to suppress suspicion, reveal the education page, or stay put) that each vendor wires at a different point: server-side redirect, form-action swap, or a managed flow with interstitial steps.

Sources:
