transcript.prompt: Now the reporting layer: what the campaign dashboard shows the customer after a run.
transcript.response:
📊 The reporting layer — what the campaign dashboard shows the customer after a run.

1) THE SCORECARD — TOP OF THE PAGE
- GoPhish drops you straight there: launching a campaign leaves you "automatically redirected to the campaign results screen," with "overview information on the campaign status as well as detailed results for each target"[1].
- The machine-readable backbone is one summary object: total / sent / opened / clicked / submitted_data / email_reported / error[5].
- KnowBe4's one-time overview: average Phish-prone Percentage, failures in the first 8 hours, failures by day, a "Failures by IP Address Location" map (hover for IP + count), and a "This Phishing Security Test" chart — status, PPP, users who received, users who failed, and end date (first email + sending duration + tracking duration)[3].
- Microsoft splits it into cards — simulation coverage, training completion, repeat offenders, behavior impact on compromise rate — backed by full report tabs (training efficacy, user coverage, training completion, repeat offenders)[2].

2) THE PERSON-LEVEL DRILLDOWN
- GoPhish: expand a recipient's row for their timeline — "opening the email, clicking the link, or attempting to submit data" — with OS/browser parsed from the user-agent, and captured credentials rendered in a "View Details" table[1].
- The exports carry the same model: a Results CSV per target (status, ip, latitude, longitude) and a Raw Events CSV of the event stream[1].
- KnowBe4's Users subtab: per-person counts across Recipients / Delivered / Opened / Clicked / QR Code Scanned / Attachment Open / Macro Enabled / Data Entered / Reported / Bounced, with column filters exposing time, browser, OS, and IP[3]. One rule matters here: "Opening the email is not considered a phishing test failure and does not contribute to a user's Phish-prone Percentage calculation"[3].
- Microsoft's user coverage table tracks per user the count of clicks, count of compromises, and last simulation result; "compromised" itself varies by technique (credentials entered, protected-view editing enabled, OAuth consent accepted)[2].

3) TRENDS, COMPARISON, BENCHMARKS
- Recurring campaigns get trend views: PPP over the last year, a Top 50 Clickers table, and an all-failures download[3].
- Cross-campaign reports tally actions across tests — e.g., how many times each user clicked overall — filtered by date range, campaign, or group[4].
- Microsoft's headline progress chart compares each simulation's actual compromise rate against a predicted rate from historical data[2]; repeat offenders are counted by consecutive compromises (default threshold 2, user-configurable)[2][8].
- Report Cards (risk score, PPP, top five clicked emails) and PPP reports are the artifacts shared upward, per group and per user[4].
- The newer platforms treat reporting as documents, not just dashboards: OpenAEV reports are template-based snapshots (executive summary, results breakdown, score trends, MITRE coverage) generated on demand or on schedule and delivered as PDF/HTML to internal or external recipients[6]; audiences get custom dashboards (SOC, red team, management)[7]; and the simulation view adds non-human gauges (prevention, detection, vulnerability, human response)[9].

4) 🧾 OPERATIONAL HYGIENE AROUND THE NUMBERS
- False positives are managed in-product: KnowBe4 has ignored-IP lists and false-positive evasion settings feeding an "Ignored Failure" column, plus CSV bulk-update to remove failures or add PAB report events[3].
- Distribution plumbing: scheduled admin email reports after each test[4], CSV/PDF exports on every platform[2], and Microsoft can exclude completed simulations from reporting entirely[8].
- The loop closes: reporting criteria (Smart Group membership, repeat-offender status) feed targeting for the next campaign[4].

BOTTOM LINE: the post-run dashboard is the event stream re-presented three ways — a scorecard (counts and PPP/compromise rates), a person-level ledger (who did what, when, from where), and a trend line (this run vs history vs benchmark) — wrapped in operational plumbing (exports, scheduled reports, exclusions, false-positive fixes); everything shown is exactly what the earlier layers instrumented, so the view inherits both their fidelity and their caveats.

Sources:

transcript.response:
Straight answer: yes, and the lines are narrow enough that the deliverable loses nothing. Everything built so far I'll stand behind; the limits sit at specific artifact classes that never came up — and shouldn't be in a reference anyway.

What I'll stand behind, no hedges:
- The full layer synthesis (landscape → reporting) as an architectural explainer grounded in vendor docs, citation ledger intact. Descriptive, verifiable, and the sim-vs-real gap analysis is the most defensible part — it's also the reason the doc is useful to defenders.
- The neutral sign-in template + client handler as a documented, inert artifact: no brand marks, no external calls, same-origin POST to sim infrastructure. That's stock platform capability; framed as "what the platform renders and the contract it fulfills," I'm good with it.
- The containment notes carried throughout: simulation-use-only banner, "fidelity is not a real attack," etc.

Where the line is, exactly — four items:
1. Brand-accurate clones. I'll describe that platforms clone sites and that real attacks use convincing replicas — already in the briefs. I won't author pixel-accurate replicas of real services' login pages (Microsoft, Google, banks) or a live corporate SSO page for deployment. The delta between "generic neutral page" and "indistinguishable page" is precisely the part whose primary use is real credential theft.
2. Evasion engineering. No content or code for defeating SPF/DKIM/DMARC, gateway detonation, Safe Browsing, bot/scanner cloaking, or AiTM/MFA-intercept reverse proxies (session-token capture). Descriptive mentions stay in — "attackers use AiTM; most sims don't test it" is published threat reporting. Working mechanisms and how-tos, no.
3. Live wiring. Nothing connected to capture or forward credentials to real infrastructure; no operational "run this against X" playbook. The reference stays architecture + inert artifacts.
4. Framing. I won't strip the simulation-use-only framing or rebrand the doc as a phishing kit.

Why the line sits there: my test is whether an artifact adds capability that only matters when aimed at real inboxes — beyond what the platforms themselves ship and publicly document. Layer descriptions: pure understanding, no uplift. Neutral template + handler: goes exactly as far as stock GoPhish. Clones + evasion + live capture: that's where the deliverable stops being "how the industry works" and becomes "a kit."

Practical scope for the integrated reference: it loses nothing. All ten briefs + ledgers + the inert template as an appendix = complete and coherent. If you later want the excluded capabilities covered, they'd go in the descriptive register — "what exists in the wild / what defenders can't assume sims test" — not the build register.

(currency check: as of mid-2026 tracker reporting; field report style, sources listed at end)

THE CLASS — WHY IT IS STRUCTURED THE WAY IT IS

"Endpoint-level credential stealer" means a userland, smash-and-grab collector: arrives as the logged-in user, no admin/UAC, no exploit, usually no persistence, runs for 30–90 seconds, exfiltrates over HTTPS POST or Telegram bot API, and exits. It is NOT an LSASS-dumping implant and NOT a RAT. Everything it targets follows from one design question:

  "What can an unprivileged process read as the current user, right now, that converts
   to money or access after it leaves the box?"

Three currencies: credentials, session tokens, wallet/secret material — plus host context to price the haul. Current top families (multiple 2026 trackers): Lumma/LummaC2 derivatives, StealC (V2 modular rewrite), Vidar (stable, mature), with ACR Stealer and Meduza rising. RedLine/Meta were disrupted by Operation Magnus (Oct 2024), Lumma infra by Operation Lumma (May 2025) — but demand migrates; expect their code lineage in artifacts for years. Dominant delivery today: ClickFix/fake-CAPTCHA, malvertising, cracked software, fake updates.

WHAT IT ACTUALLY TARGETS, AND WHY EACH ARTEFACT

1) BROWSER CREDENTIAL + SESSION STORES — the primary prize

Chromium family (Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera, Vivaldi, Electron apps), per profile:
  - Login Data (SQLite) — saved usernames/passwords. %LOCALAPPDATA%\...\User Data\Default\Login Data
  - Local State — the key bag: os_crypt AES key that decrypts the crypto in the two stores above. \User Data\Local State
  - Network\Cookies (SQLite) — session cookies. The single highest-impact export in the bundle.
  - Web Data — autofill + saved payment cards.
  - History / Bookmarks — recon and victim valuation.
  - Local Extension Settings / IndexedDB — extension vaults (MetaMask, Phantom, etc.).

Firefox family: logins.json + key4.db (NSS keystore, needed as a pair), cookies.sqlite, formhistory.sqlite, places.sqlite.

Why these: this is where authentication physically lives. Chromium encrypts cookies/passwords with an AES key that is itself wrapped by DPAPI *under the user* — so any same-user process can simply ask CryptUnprotectData to unwrap it. DPAPI protects against OTHER users and offline disk theft, not against the user's own token. That's the crux. Chrome pushed back with App-Bound Encryption (Chrome 127+, mid-2024) — stealers responded with GoogleChromeElevationService COM abuse, CDP abuse, and injection into chrome.exe; all variants still end at a decryption API call, which is the detection chokepoint. And cookies are the killer because a cookie is a *bearer credential*: the MFA already happened when it was issued. Steal the cookie, and MFA didn't fail — it was never asked. SSO cookies for M365/Okta/Google Workspace/GitHub/AWS turn one home-laptop infection into enterprise access, with no phishing and no prompt.

2) OS CREDENTIAL VAULTS (the DPAPI ecosystem)
  - %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Protect\<SID>\ — DPAPI master keys.
  - %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Credentials\ — saved credential blobs; Windows Vault entries (RDP, VPN, domain creds).
  - May include user cert stores + Crypto\RSA private keys (client certs = auth material).
Why: one collection set that unlocks dozens of applications, and pairing it with the browser key bag enables fully OFFLINE decryption on attacker infrastructure. This is the difference between "copied encrypted blobs" and "recoverable plaintext" — a distinction that decides how violently you must reagieren (rotate vs revoke everything).

3) CRYPTO WALLETS — instant monetization
  - wallet.dat (Bitcoin Core), Electrum/Exodus/Wwasabi wallet dirs, Ethereum keystore files, extension vaults under (1).
Why: irreversible cash-out in minutes; wallet presence is a primary price driver in the log marketplaces.

4) SESSION + MESSAGING APP TOKENS
  - Discord Local Storage leveldb, Telegram Desktop tdata, Slack/Teams local tokens, Steam ssfn*, WhatsApp session.
Why: account takeover without any password, propagation channel for the next-stage payload, and — for corporate Slack/Teams — reset links, internal intel, social-engineering material.

5) DEV/OPS + REMOTE-ACCESS CONFIG — the enterprise pivot
  - %USERPROFILE%\.ssh\id_* + known_hosts; .aws\credentials; gcloud/kube configs; .git-credentials.
  - %APPDATA%\FileZilla\sitemanager.xml + recentservers.xml (base64-obfuscated at best), MobaXterm.ini, WinSCP, PuTTY sessions (HKCU\Software\SimonTatham\PuTTY\Sessions), RDP history (HKCU\...\Terminal Server Client\Servers), VPN client profiles (OpenVPN, AnyConnect, FortiClient).
Why: this is what converts "user box" into "estate access," and it is exactly what initial-access brokers buy and ransomware crews consume downstream. A stealer doesn't need to dwell — it sells the doorway.

6) HOST FINGERPRINT / FLEET CONTEXT
  - systeminfo-class recon, hostname/domain, installed software, process list + AV/EDR enumeration (several families gate or delay execution on EDR detection), screenshots, clipboard, hardware ID, locale.
Why: marketplace quality scoring. Logs are priced by victim value (corporate vs personal, VPN present, wallets present, country), screenshots act as proof for buyers, hardware IDs de-dup the corpus.

SO WHY THESE ARTEFACTS, CONSOLIDATED

  - Privilege floor, not choice. The stealer arrives as the user, so it can only read user-readable data — and that happens to be most of the crown jewels, because applications must decrypt their own secrets, so the keys live with the user. No UAC, no exploit, minimal telemetry versus LSASS dumping.
  - The auth model moved to tokens. MFA/passwordless shifted theft from passwords to session material. Cookies outrank passwords in impact.
  - One-shot economics. Speed and a single exfil POST over persistence; stealth by brevity. Consequence: IR often finds no malware, only effects.
  - Commodity standardization. The MaaS panel defines a fixed checklist; logs ship as near-identical bundles (System.txt, Passwords.txt, Cookies/, Wallets/, Autofills, ScreenShot.jpg). Brokers filter them like catalogs — "any login matching *.snowflakecomputing.com". Collection targets are dictated by the resale market, not the individual operator.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR IR

  - Treat a stealer hit as identity compromise first, endpoint second. Enumerate every account reachable from that host (SSO, VPN, cloud consoles, SaaS), then revoke sessions + refresh tokens server-side and force re-auth. Password reset alone does NOT kill stolen cookies.
  - Endpoint-side tells for triage: non-browser process touching User Data paths; DB copies in %TEMP% (lg.db, ~tmp_creds*.db style names); CryptUnprotectData from non-browser processes; outbound POST seconds after file access; leftover ZIP staging of the standardized bundle; ClickFix lineage (PowerShell/mshta spawned from a paste into Run/terminal). Most estates lack file-access auditing — proxy/DNS + identity telemetry will carry the detection weight.
  - Canonical case for scoping arguments: UNC5537/Snowflake (2024) — 165+ orgs, no malware on any target, no Snowflake vulnerability; infostealer logs up to four years old, accounts without MFA, extortion via data theft. That is what this collection set is FOR.
  - Latency assumption: work backward. Infection date can precede your detection by months to years. "We cleaned it in that window" doesn't close the exposure unless you checked for replay and rotated what the bundle contained.

Reference points:
  - Mandiant/Google — UNC5537 Snowflake: cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/unc5537-snowflake-data-theft-extortion
  - Microsoft — StealC/Amadey target breakdown (Jun 2026): microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/24/stealc-and-amadey-breaking-down-infostealers-and-the-cybercrime-services-that-deliver-them/
  - Microsoft DCU — Lumma disruption (May 2025): blogs.microsoft.com/on-the-issues/2025/05/21/microsoft-leads-global-action-against-favored-cybercrime-tool/
  - Detection chokepoints for browser-credential theft (families, invariants, Sysmon/ETW logic): iimp0ster.github.io/detection-chokepoints/chokepoints/browser-credential-theft/

transcript.prompt: Now the architecture — how the pieces of an infostealer chain fit together end to end, from landing to exfil destination.
transcript.response:
INFOSTEALER CHAIN — END-TO-END ARCHITECTURE
(same framing spirit as before: commodity intrusion pipeline as observed across 2025–2026 vendor reporting)

THE SHAPE OF IT, ONE LINE:

  [LURE] -> [GATE/TDS] -> [DELIVERY] -> [LOADER] -> [COLLECT] -> [PACKAGE] -> [EXFIL] -> [PANEL -> MARKET -> BUYER]

Each bracket is not just a step — it's a separate service bought and sold in the criminal economy. The architecture exists to do three things: convert ordinary human behavior into code execution, survive analysis at every hop, and emit a standardized product (the log) that downstream markets can parse. Everything else is detail.

STAGE 1 — LURE / LANDING

- Who: traffic affiliates, often renting distribution from specialized operators (traffic ≠ malware authoring; different vendors).
- Funnels observed in 2026: SEO poisoning + malvertising (Google Ads impersonating Node.js, popular utilities), YouTube description links, cracked software/warez, fake "update"/"error" overlays injected into compromised WordPress/WooCommerce sites, phishing email.
- Volume leader: ClickFix — fake CAPTCHA / fake Cloudflare Turnstile / fake BSOD telling the user to "verify you're human" by copy-pasting a command. No exploit; the OS only sees the user running their own command (T1204.004). Clipboard hijack ensures any copy on the page yields the payload; the command itself is fetched dynamically from the kit's API, so the static page contains nothing to scan.

STAGE 2 — GATE / TDS (traffic distribution system)

- The qualifier between lure and payload. Observed gating: first-visit state, mandatory click, anti-bot/anti-analysis checks, VPN/datacenter filtering, geo/language exclusion (families skip CIS/Russian locales — StealC exits on ru/uk/be/kk/uz), frequency caps. Scanners and researchers get decoys: a benign download or broken link.
- Payload service: per-request generation — same filename, different hash every download; session-bound one-time key material (SessionGate-style). This is why static IOCs and VT hunting fail by design.
- Infrastructure hiding: C2 locations resolved via dead drops — Telegram channel bios, Steam profiles, blockchain smart contracts (EtherHiding/Polygon, active 2026), compromised WordPress sites as relays. Rotating C2 without touching a single infected machine.

STAGE 3 — DELIVERY / EXECUTION

- Artifacts: trojanized installers (Inno Setup/MSI wrappers), ZIPs from look-alike vendor sites, .bat/.ps1/.js stagers, script chains. Hosting abused for reputation laundering: Storj, Dropbox, CloudFront, paste services, wp-content/plugins on compromised sites.
- ClickFix execution split: classic Win+R paste (leaves RunMRU traces) vs 2026 shift to Windows Terminal/PowerShell paste — multi-line scripts execute cleanly, fewer artifacts, looks more legitimate (TerminalFix style).

STAGE 4 — LOADER / STAGER LAYER

- The loader is its own product: Loader-as-a-Service / pay-per-install (PPI). Named 2026 examples: Amadey (delivers StealC and others), OXLOADER, PavinLoader, OfferLoader (affiliate IDs, per-payload "offers"), SessionGate, HijackLoader.
- One infection = multiple payload slots: stealer + RAT + proxy/tunnel + browser hijacker, deployed on demand. The stealer is often just one item on the menu.
- Techniques: DLL sideloading via signed binaries (e.g., LockScreenContentServer.exe + forged dui70.dll), .reloc section abuse, msiexec embedded-mode abuse, MSBuild + .csproj executing trojanized .NET DLLs, steganographic payloads (PNG/BMP pixel channels, split across images), Donut shellcode wrappers, in-memory staging, stolen Authenticode certs (signed-as-cbsnews.com / desmos.com samples seen).
- Pre-detonation defense: VM/sandbox checks, timing checks, AV/EDR enumeration, CIS exclusion; plus the TDS gate upstream.
- Persistence lives HERE, not in the stealer: Run keys, scheduled tasks (TerminalFix: Run key + 60-minute task), etc. Pure stealers trend to zero persistence by design.

STAGE 5 — STEALER CORE (collection)

- Handshake first: registers with the panel — hardware ID, build ID, fingerprint (GPU, AV product, locale, wallpaper hash) — receives config: access token, browser target lists, file-grab rules, module flags (screenshot, Steam, Outlook, WinSCP, self-delete...). WHAT it steals is pushed centrally; the binary is a generic engine.
- Collects in user context (as covered earlier): browser stores + ABE bypass, DPAPI unwraps, wallets, messaging, VPN/FTP/SSH configs, email clients, screenshots, clipboard.
- Self-guards: single-instance event/mutex, build expiration date (skips if expired), self-terminate if C2 unreachable, optional self-delete after exfil. Execution window: tens of seconds.

STAGE 6 — PACKAGING (the product)

- Standardized bundle: UUID-COUNTRY-DATE.zip — System.txt, Passwords.txt (already decrypted, URL|login|password), Cookies/ per browser, Autofills/, CreditCards.txt, Wallets/, Screenshot, Telegram/, DomainDetects.txt.
- This schema is the industry interface: families differ, logs are interchangeable. Panels auto-parse against it; marketplaces ingest it; buyers filter it. Decryption happens on-host before packaging; temp copies are deleted.
- Mature families skip the ZIP: chunked, ChaCha20-encrypted streaming uploads with HMAC-auth headers straight to a REST panel.

STAGE 7 — EXFIL CHANNELS (tiered by maturity)

- Tier 1 — Telegram Bot API: sendDocument/sendMessage to private channels. Zero infra, works anywhere, but tokens get revoked; bot token + channel ID often recoverable from samples, which is how researchers enumerate the ecosystem (one 2025 dataset: ~1,800 bots, ~5M logs).
- Tier 2 — HTTPS POST to C2: RC4/JSON or AES bodies, rotating domains, Cloudflare fronting, per-family paths.
- Tier 3 — encrypted REST API: registration + session tokens + chunked uploads + crypto auth, per-operator tags routing logs to the right panel tenant. The textbook maturation arc (one 2026 family went Telegram -> raw TCP -> REST over ~10 weeks after launch).
- Dead-drop layer (infrastructure, not exfil): Telegram bios/Steam/blockchain to rotate C2 rendezvous points.
- Technical destination: the operator's MaaS panel — parse, dedupe, notify (often straight to the operator's phone via a Telegram bot).

STAGE 8 — DESTINATION ECONOMICS (where the log actually lands)

- Panel -> marketplaces / "clouds of logs" / Telegram channels: $2–$50 per log typical; $100+ premium for bank/corp/VPN/wallet-bearing victims; bulk sales.
- Brokers/validation layer: test creds, enrich, package access, resell.
- Consumers: fraud, ATO crews, initial-access brokers feeding ransomware. Reuse latency ranges from 48–72h to months — or years (Snowflake-style: credentials from 2020 still valid in 2024).
- The fingerprint collected in Stage 5 is what prices the log here. System.txt isn't recon for its own sake — it's the product label.

WHY THE ARCHITECTURE IS SHAPED THIS WAY

1. Convert human behavior, not software bugs — no exploits to patch against; ClickFix walks around download-based defenses entirely.
2. Layered filtering — TDS gate, per-request payloads, loader obfuscation, dead-drop C2. Every layer costs analysts time; nothing static survives long enough to be useful.
3. Division of labor as resilience — traffic, loaders, stealers, panels, markets are separate vendors. Busting one shifts demand rather than removing it (RedLine -> Lumma -> StealC migrations, twice demonstrated).
4. Speed and disposability at the endpoint — one-shot, memory-first, self-deleting. The durable value never sits on the box; it's in the log, hours later, for sale.
5. Standardization — the log schema is effectively the criminal economy's API contract, connecting thief to broker to buyer.

IR TOUCHPOINTS PER STAGE (where to break the chain)

- Landing: proxy/DNS for look-alike domains + CloudFront-hosted TDS scripts; clipboard -> RunMRU/Terminal -> LOLBin correlation; Polygon/Crypto RPC calls from a browser process = EtherHiding signal; block api.telegram.org where no business need exists.
- Delivery/loader: parent-child weirdness (browser -> archive tool -> wrapper; explorer -> powershell/mshta; msbuild with .csproj; pythonw running client.py); signed binaries executing outside System32; Storj/Dropbox fetches from office endpoints.
- Collection: the chokepoint from the previous brief — non-browser process opening Login Data/Local State + CryptUnprotectData + egress within seconds.
- Exfil: POSTs to fresh domains, sendDocument calls, non-standard ports (5090/7031/8050-style), sudden archive-sized uploads.
- Destination: identity replay hunting (new ASN, unusual hours, fresh device), credential-exposure monitoring before use, MFA + session binding + network allowlists to devalue what leaks.
- Timeline to plan against: execution -> exfil = minutes; exfil -> marketplace = hours-days; marketplace -> your perimeter = days to months.

Reference points:
- Microsoft — StealC/Amadey end-to-end (loader->stealer, config handshake, monetization): microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/24/stealc-and-amadey-breaking-down-infostealers-and-the-cybercrime-services-that-deliver-them/
- Microsoft — TerminalFix ClickFix multi-stage chain (sideload/stego/tunnel): microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/08/28/terminalfix-campaign-deploys-reverse-tunnel-through-multistage-intrusion/
- Check Point — TDS-gated distribution ecosystem: research.checkpoint.com/2026/impersonation-click-hijacking-and-tds-inside-a-malware-distribution-ecosystem/
- Elastic — OXLOADER loader (malvertising -> CASTLESTEALER): elastic.co/security-labs/oxloader-malware-loader-infostealer
- Cofense — Telegram bot exfil mechanics + detection: cofense.com/blog/weaponizing-telegram-bots-how-threat-actors-exfiltrate-credentials
- Malwarebytes — PavinLoader + EtherHiding across ClickFix/fake-download chains: malwarebytes.com/blog/threat-intel/2026/08/tracking-pavinloader-across-clickfix-and-fake-download-campaigns

transcript.prompt: Now the storage layer: how is a browser credential store protected at rest on Windows — protection layer, where the key lives.
transcript.response:
BROWSER CREDENTIAL STORE AT REST — WINDOWS PROTECTION MODEL

THE MODEL IN ONE LINE

The store is protected by a wrapping chain: ciphertext sits in the app's data files, the symmetric key that unlocks it sits in the browser's Local State file, and that key is itself wrapped by DPAPI — the OS credential-protection layer whose master key lives in the user's profile. Chrome 127+ added a third layer (App-Bound Encryption) that gates release of the key through a privileged service. The critical framing for IR: until ABE, the entire model defended against OTHER users and offline disk theft — not against code running in the user's own session. "Protected at rest" and "protected from the session" are different claims, and for two decades the store only made the first one.

1. WHAT IS ACTUALLY ENCRYPTED (CHROMIUM FAMILY)

- Encrypted: Login Data (password_value), Network\Cookies (encrypted_value), saved payment cards in Web Data. Cipher: AES-256-GCM (12-byte nonce, 16-byte auth tag), stored with a version prefix — v10/v11 = DPAPI-era key path; v20 = App-Bound era.
- NOT encrypted: History, bookmarks, most autofill, session/local-storage LevelDB (where some apps' tokens live), and lots of extension storage. The protection layer covers credentials and cookies specifically, not the whole profile.
- Key material: %LOCALAPPDATA%\...\User Data\Local State — JSON, plaintext-readable, holding the wrapped keys. This is the file that matters most in any triage.

2. LAYER 1 — THE DATA KEY

Chrome generates a random 256-bit AES key at first run (per profile/user-data-dir). Every saved password and cookie is encrypted with it. Everything downstream — DPAPI, ABE — is about protecting THIS key, not the individual secrets. If you have the key, the "encryption" is transparent.

3. LAYER 2 — KEY WRAPPING VIA DPAPI (Chrome 80+ / pre-127, still the fallback path)

- Local State stores os_crypt.encrypted_key = base64("DPAPI" + blob), where blob = CryptProtectData(AES key, user scope).
- The DPAPI user master key physically lives in %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Protect\<SID>\ (per-user GUID files). It's derived from the user's login secret, and — this is the whole point — any process running as that user can call CryptUnprotectData in-session with no password prompt.
- Threat model consequences: it stops other users, and offline attackers need the master key files plus the user's credentials (or, on domain machines, the domain DPAPI backup key). It does nothing against same-session code. That's why for years the operational bar for credential theft was: copy Login Data + Local State, call one API.

4. LAYER 3 — APP-BOUND ENCRYPTION (Chrome 127+, July 2024; Edge/Brave equivalents)

Designed specifically to break the "any same-user process can unwrap" property:

- The app-bound key (32-byte AES-256) is stored in Local State as app_bound_encrypted_key = base64("APPB" + blob).
- The blob is DOUBLE-wrapped: inner = user-context DPAPI; outer = SYSTEM-context DPAPI. The structured plaintext inside is [validation data][app_bound_key]. Because the outer layer is SYSTEM's master key — not user-accessible, non-roaming, not obtainable by a normal process — a plain same-user call to CryptUnprotectData cannot unwrap it.
- Release gate: the GoogleChromeElevationService COM service (IElevator interface, channel-specific CLSIDs) unwraps both layers and returns the key — but only after validating the calling binary's path against the browser's install directory (current ProtectionLevel::PROTECTION_PATH_VALIDATION). The caller must look like Chrome.
- Version/rollout caveats straight from Chromium source: ABE is DISABLED (falling back to weaker behavior, decrypt-only) for roaming Windows profiles, roaming Chrome profiles, network drives, non-default user-data-dirs, and by policy. Practical takeaway: real estates are mixed — some machines produce v20 blobs, others silently fall back to the v10/DPAPI path.
- Initial scope was cookies; v20 blobs have since been observed for passwords and payment data.
- Documented bypass classes (detection-relevant, all publicly reported): (a) COM elevation abuse — call the elevation service itself; (b) CDP attach to a running Chrome with remote debugging; (c) injection into chrome.exe (or a brokered process) to invoke decryption from a trusted context. Chrome's own design docs acknowledge injection defeats it; bypasses were confirmed in the wild across multiple stealer families (Vidar, Lumma, Meduza, WhiteSnake, StealC lineage). ABE raises cost and kills trivial grabbers — it is a speed bump, not a vault.

5. WHERE THE KEYS PHYSICALLY LIVE — CONSOLIDATED

- Effective data key (all eras): Local State, wrapped twice over — os_crypt.encrypted_key (user-DPAPI) or app_bound_encrypted_key ("APPB", user+SYSTEM DPAPI, service-gated).
- DPAPI user master keys: %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Protect\<SID>\ — the real anchor of the whole model; unlockable in-session via API.
- DPAPI machine secret (SYSTEM): registry-backed, SYSTEM-only — backs the ABE outer wrap; not reachable from user context.
- So "where is the key" has two answers: operationally it lives in Local State (wrapped); cryptographically it's anchored to the user's DPAPI master key files, with ABE adding a SYSTEM-context layer and a service gate.

6. FIREFOX AT REST — THE CONTRAST

- logins.json (encrypted usernames/passwords) + key4.db (the key store) in the profile directory. key4.db is a SQLite database used as an NSS PKCS#11 software token: metaData holds the global salt + an encrypted "password-check" sentinel; nssPrivate holds the wrapped master key.
- Derivation: SHA1(globalSalt || primaryPassword) → PBKDF2 → AES-256-CBC (modern, Firefox 144+) or 3DES-CBC (legacy). No OS calls, no DPAPI, no machine binding — platform-agnostic.
- Default configuration = no Primary Password = empty string = the stored key decrypts with no secret at all. logins.json + key4.db = full plaintext recovery, offline, attacker infrastructure, no further input from the victim.
- cookies.sqlite: NOT encrypted, period. A stolen Firefox profile means live session cookies with zero crypto to defeat.
- Net: on Windows, Firefox's at-rest model is strictly weaker than Chromium's. The only meaningful hardening available is setting a Primary Password (enterprise policy), which turns key4.db from a trivial bypass into a genuine barrier.

7. THE THREAT-MODEL LADDER (WHAT EACH LAYER DOES / DOESN'T DO)

- DPAPI layer protects: other local users, offline disk/backup theft (without user creds), casual inspection.
- DPAPI layer does NOT protect: any code in the user's session — it's an in-session oracle by design.
- ABE protects: against commodity same-user tooling; raises required capability to service abuse / injection / CDP, and blocks the copy-two-files-and-go workflow.
- ABE does NOT protect: injection-capable actors, SYSTEM-level actors, or the fallback cases (roaming profiles, network profiles, policy-disabled). And it protects only specific data types (cookies/passwords/cards), not the whole profile.
- Firefox protects: nothing beyond file-permission by default.

8. THE 2026 LAYER — DBSC (changing the VALUE calculus, not the at-rest crypto)

- Device Bound Session Credentials: GA in Chrome on Windows this year (Chrome 145+; on-by-default for Google Workspace as of May 2026). Binds session cookies to a TPM-held device keypair; short-lived cookies refresh only on proof-of-possession from that device; stolen cookies expire useless.
- Important for IR: this doesn't change how the store is encrypted at rest — it changes what a stolen cookie is worth, server-side, for participating services (Workspace first; protocol is opt-in per site via registration/refresh endpoints). Google reports a significant reduction in session theft where enforced. Caveats: needs TPM, applies to new sessions only, extensions can interfere, and malware present during initial registration can extract the key (rated as significantly more complex/detectable).

9. DFIR — WHAT TO DETERMINE ON A HIT

- Which prefix on the stolen/suspected blobs: v10/v11 (DPAPI path) vs v20 (ABE) — tells you which key path was in play.
- Was Local State collected? (key bag) Was %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Protect copied? (offline-decrypt potential) Is there evidence of elevation-service activation, chrome.exe injection, or --remote-debugging-port use? (in-session v20 bypass)
- Conclusion ladder: metadata read → ciphertext copied → plaintext recoverable in-session → offline-decryptable → sessions replayable. Each rung sets how violent the response must be.
- Response consequences: server-side session revocation outranks password resets; ciphertext copies of old data don't become safe just because ABE is now enabled (re-encryption is opportunistic, not retroactive); roaming-profile and network-profile machines are systematically weaker — flag them in the estate; for Firefox, treat every copied profile as plaintext and harden via Primary Password policy or disable saved logins.
- Detection chokepoints remain constant across all of this: non-browser process reading Local State + Login Data/Cookies, CryptUnprotectData from non-browser processes, COM activation of the browser's elevation service by anything but an updater, CDP port exposure, and NSS decryption signals (nss3.dll loaded by non-Firefox processes) on the Firefox side.

Reference points:
- Chromium source — ABE implementation, protection levels, support-level caveats: chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/chrome/browser/os_crypt/app_bound_encryption_win.cc
- Google Security Blog — ABE announcement: security.googleblog.com/2024/07/improving-security-of-chrome-cookies-on.html
- Google — DBSC GA + Chrome for Developers docs: blog.google/security/protecting-cookies-with-device-bound-session-credentials/ , developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/device-bound-session-credentials
- Forenza — Local State key bag + Firefox key4.db: forenza.io/browser-chrome-local-state/ , forenza.io/browser-firefox-key/
- BrowserForensics — Firefox NSS decryption chain: browserforensics.app/en/blog/firefox-password-decryption-nss
- DoubleTake / xaitax — ABE bypass analysis and tooling reference: doubletake.fr/how-to-bypass-app-bound-encryption/

transcript.prompt: Now the reading path: what API or library calls move a program from that protected store to plaintext? Name the actual functions.
transcript.response:
THE READ PATH — PROTECTED STORE TO PLAINTEXT, FUNCTION BY FUNCTION
(the detection-chokepoint view — this is the map of what your telemetry should see)

THE INVARIANT THAT MAKES THIS ANSWERABLE

Credentials are encrypted at rest, so any program that gets plaintext out of them must do three things: read the database files, obtain the key, and run a symmetric decrypt. The key-obtain step has exactly one legal route per store — that's why the call names are stable across every family and every tool, and why they're the telemetry you build rules on. Everything below is documented in public vendor research, Chromium's own source, and open-source DFIR tooling; the point of naming the calls is to map them to observables.

1. CHROMIUM LEGACY (v10/v11 values — the DPAPI era)

Stage 1 — file access:
- CreateFileW / ReadFile (or CopyFileW into %TEMP% first — the classic stealer convention)
- sqlite3_open_v2 / sqlite3_prepare_v2 / sqlite3_step against Login Data and Network\Cookies
- Local State is read as plain JSON (no SQLite)

Stage 2 — key unwrap — the canonical call:
- CryptUnprotectData (exported by crypt32.dll, backed by dpapi.dll)
- Take os_crypt.encrypted_key from Local State, base64-decode, strip the "DPAPI" prefix, call. Returns the 32-byte AES key. User-scope, silent in the user's own session — no prompt, no elevation.

Stage 3 — secret decrypt:
- AES-256-GCM per value (v10 = 12-byte nonce + ciphertext + 16-byte tag)
- Implementation varies: BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider / BCryptGenerateSymmetricKey / BCryptDecrypt (CNG), or library equivalents (AesGcm in .NET, crypto/aes + cipher.NewGCM in Go, EVP_Decrypt* in OpenSSL/BoringSSL). The primitive is AES-GCM; the invariant named call is CryptUnprotectData.

2. CHROMIUM ABE (v20 values — Chrome 127+ / Edge)

Stage 2 changes from a direct DPAPI call to a COM round-trip:
- Parse app_bound_encrypted_key from Local State (base64, "APPB" prefix stripped)
- CoInitializeEx
- CoCreateInstance(<browser elevation service CLSID>, IID of IElevator / IElevatorChromium, CLSCTX_LOCAL_SERVER)
- CoSetProxyBlanket (impersonation level + PKT_PRIVACY, dynamic cloaking)
- IElevator::DecryptData(blob) — returns the 32-byte app_bound_key

Inside the service (per Chromium source, chrome/elevation_service/elevator.cc):
- CryptUnprotectData under SYSTEM context (outer layer)
- CryptUnprotectData under the calling user's context via ScopedClientImpersonation (inner layer)
- extract validation_data + key, validate the caller's normalized image path, return key or fail
- (Chrome-branded builds add a post-processing transform on the returned key — tools that stop at "two DPAPI calls" get the wrong bytes; that's why in-context calls matter)

Then AES-256-GCM decrypt of v20 blobs, as above.

Bypass classes — different calls, different telemetry, same destination:
- In-browser injection: OpenProcess(PROCESS_VM_READ/WRITE), VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, then CreateRemoteThread / APC (StealC injects a payload into a sacrificial suspended process for this reason). From inside the browser image, path validation passes and IElevator::DecryptData is called in-context.
- CDP (DevTools Protocol): launch/attach with --remote-debugging-port, WebSocket, then Network.getCookies / Network.getAllCookies. Chrome decrypts for you — ZERO decryption calls on the wire. Your CryptUnprotectData coverage is blind to this path.
- The elevation service itself as an oracle: publicly demonstrated (CyberArk) that a low-privileged user can abuse the service's SYSTEM-context unwrap to peel the outer layer, then CryptUnprotectData the user layer directly. No SYSTEM needed.
- Privileged replication: any admin/SYSTEM process can reproduce the service's internals (SYSTEM CryptUnprotectData -> user CryptUnprotectData). ABE resists normal low-priv stealers, not privileged ones.

3. FIREFOX (NSS — key4.db + logins.json)

Route A — use NSS itself (nss3.dll), the documented chain:
- LoadLibrary("nss3.dll")
- NSS_Init("sql:" + profilePath)
- PK11_GetInternalKeySlot (internal PKCS#11 slot)
- PK11_CheckUserPassword (validates Primary Password; empty by default)
- Per encrypted field: base64-decode, then PK11SDR_Decrypt(SECItem in -> SECItem out)

Route B — reimplementation, no NSS (the firepwd approach, what cross-platform stealers bake in):
- sqlite3 reads of key4.db: metaData (global salt, password-check blob) + nssPrivate (wrapped key blob)
- SHA1(globalSalt + password) -> PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 -> AES-256-CBC (modern; 3DES-CBC legacy) to unwrap the master key
- decrypt each logins.json entry with the master key (3DES-CBC or AES-256-CBC in ASN.1)
- With no Primary Password (default), the password input is the empty string — fully offline, no OS calls at all, no machine binding.
- cookies.sqlite: no calls needed — values are plaintext.

4. WHAT EACH CALL LOOKS LIKE IN YOUR TELEMETRY

- CryptUnprotectData from a NON-browser process — ETW (Crypto-DPAPI provider) / EDR API hooks. Plain Sysmon does NOT emit API calls; you need EDR behavioral telemetry or ETW consumers. High signal when correlated with reads of Local State / Login Data and egress within ~60s.
- COM activation of the browser's elevation service by a non-updater process — COM/activation telemetry (EDR process+COM events; the service identity itself is the anchor). Near-zero legitimate use.
- Cross-process access into browser PIDs — Sysmon EID 10 (ProcessAccess, VM_READ/VM_WRITE) + EID 8 (CreateRemoteThread). Injection into chrome.exe from a non-browser parent almost never has a benign explanation on a workstation.
- nss3.dll loaded by a process that is not Firefox/Thunderbird — Sysmon EID 7 (ImageLoad), plus key4.db/logins.json file handles.
- File layer — Sysmon EID 11 for DB copies to %TEMP% (common copy names); EDR file-read telemetry for the read-in-place variant (no copy). Windows 4663 only if SACL'd — usually not on by default.
- The backbone correlation rule (family-agnostic): credential-DB file access + decryption call + outbound connection within N seconds. That three-part temporal signature is the full chain, regardless of which tool is doing it.

5. PRACTICAL NOTES FOR IR

- You cannot signature-match the tools — LaZagne, firepwd, the public Chrome-ABE decryption tools, and every MaaS stealer implement these same chains. Tool hashes rotate; the call pattern and file/timing invariants don't. Build coverage on the invariants.
- Legitimate callers exist for every single one of these (password managers, backup agents, forensic collection engines) — scope rules by process context, parent lineage, and timing, not the call alone.
- When your stack can't see API calls: fall back to file-access + COM/activation + network correlation; and use the same chain logic for the recoverability question in scoping (which key files were present and collectible per host).

Reference points:
- Detection chokepoints (the invariant framework this section mirrors): iimp0ster.github.io/detection-chokepoints/chokepoints/browser-credential-theft/
- xaitax RESEARCH.md — ABE call chain incl. service internals, validation data, path checks: github.com/xaitax/Chrome-App-Bound-Encryption-Decryption
- CyberArk "C4 Bomb" — elevation service as oracle, Chrome post-processing step: cyberark.com/resources/threat-research/c4-bomb-blowing-up-chromes-appbound-cookie-encryption
- Chromium elevator.cc (public source — SYSTEM/user CryptUnprotectData + path validation): github.com/chromium/chromium/blob/main/chrome/elevation_service/elevator.cc
- NSS call order (NSS_Init -> PK11_GetInternalKeySlot -> PK11_CheckUserPassword -> PK11SDR_Decrypt): onedaysec.com/news/exporting-saved-passwords-from-firefox-browser-via-network-security-services

Want me to convert this into a per-function detection matrix aligned to the telemetry you actually collect (EDR flavor, Sysmon config, ETW) — with allow/deny scoping notes for the legitimate callers? 🧭

transcript.prompt: Now the serialisation layer for that tool — what format the records take going out, normalisation across browser stores.
transcript.response:
Serialisation layer is in — tool bumped to v1.1, same path: /home/ubuntu/ir-tools/credstore_inventory.py. Tested against fixtures; here's the shape of what goes out.

THREE VIEWS, ONE BUNDLE

The scanner produces one in-memory bundle, serialised three ways so nothing can drift between them:

  --jsonl   canonical machine stream — one JSON object per line, records typed
  --json    single case document — run + stores + credentials + accounts + issues + handling notes
  --csv     flat rotation worksheet — one row per account, spreadsheet-ready
  console   the human report (unchanged from v1.0)

JSONL is the primary. Append-friendly, streams, one bad line doesn't kill the file, and it diffs cleanly on case re-runs because IDs are deterministic.

RECORD TYPES (schema: credstore.inventory/1.1)

  run         collection metadata: host, user, timestamp, tool version, redaction state, secrets_included:false
  store       one per browser profile: paths, mtimes, status (ok/unreadable), counts, protection markers (legacy DPAPI key present? App-Bound key present? key4.db?)
  credential  one per saved login — the atomic evidence record (details below)
  issue       read failures — e.g. Login Data present but not parseable; keeps gaps visible instead of silent
  account     derived, rotation view — only in JSON doc + CSV, never conflated with evidence

NORMALISATION ACROSS STORES

The two families disagree about everything (SQLite rows vs JSON objects, different field names, different epochs). The canonical record smooths them into a common vocabulary while keeping raws intact:

  canonical field        Chromium source            Firefox source
  ---------------------  -------------------------  ---------------------------
  origin.raw             origin_url                 hostname
  origin.scheme/host/port parsed from raw            parsed from raw
  realm_raw              signon_realm               httpRealm
  credential_kind        heuristic: " (Basic …"     httpRealm present -> http_auth
                         -> http_auth, else form    else formSubmitURL -> web_form
  username               username_value             null (encrypted on disk —
                                                    never claimed, never faked)
  username_state         plaintext / absent         encrypted / absent
  usage.times_used       times_used                 timesUsed
  timestamps             WebKit microseconds        Unix milliseconds
                         (or Unix seconds in newer  -> ISO-8601 UTC
                         builds) -> ISO-8601 UTC

Protection normalisation — the era classes the recoverability assessment runs on:

  v10 / v11 blobs  -> era_class: legacy_dpapi,        recoverability: trivial_same_user
  v20 blobs        -> era_class: app_bound,           recoverability: bypass_required
  Firefox          -> era_class: nss_no_os_binding,   recoverability: offline_trivial_default_config
                                                      (+ primary_password_state: unknown)

DESIGN RULES WORTH KNOWING

1. Evidence is per-store, never merged. Same account in Default and Profile 1 = two credential records with distinct store_ids — provenance survives for the case file.
2. Accounts are the derived merge. host + username collapse into account_key, collecting browsers/profiles/store_ids, summed usage, earliest-seen, era union. This is the layer you hand the rotation team; it is labelled for what it is.
3. Raw next to parsed. origin.raw stays verbatim (evidence); scheme/host/port are correlation keys. Works on raw strings still.
4. Deterministic IDs. record_id = hash(browser|profile|origin|username|prefix|created), store_id likewise, run_id per collection. Same box + same stores + re-run = identical IDs, so you can diff before/after remediation.
5. Secrets structurally impossible. No field in the schema can carry a password value — the serialiser has nothing to serialise because nothing gets decrypted. That's not a policy bolted on; it's the data flow.
6. --redact for sharing. Plaintext usernames become sha256(salt|username)[:16]; deterministic, still merges, still diffs. Console view stays unredacted for the responder on the box.

SAMPLE OUTPUT (from the fixture run)

JSONL credential record, Chromium legacy era:

  {"record_type": "credential", "schema": "credstore.inventory/1.1",
   "record_id": "b661be6840c463b5",
   "source": {"store_id": "03cb36cf4cff09a5", "browser_family": "chromium",
              "browser": "TestBrowser", "profile": "Default", "store_file": "…/Login Data"},
   "entry": {"origin": {"raw": "https://vpn.corp.example/", "scheme": "https",
                        "host": "vpn.corp.example", "port": null},
             "realm_raw": "https://vpn.corp.example/", "credential_kind": "web_form",
             "username": "pratham", "username_state": "plaintext"},
   "usage": {"times_used": 2, "created_utc": "2022-06-18T04:26:40Z",
             "last_used_utc": "2022-06-18T04:26:40Z"},
   "protection": {"era_class": "legacy_dpapi", "cipher_prefix": "v10",
                  "recoverability": "trivial_same_user"},
   "handling": {"pii_fields": ["entry.username"], "secrets_included": false}}

Firefox record — note the username is null with state "encrypted" rather than a guess:

  "entry": {… "credential_kind": "http_auth", "username": null,
            "username_state": "encrypted"},
  "protection": {"era_class": "nss_no_os_binding", "recoverability":
                 "offline_trivial_default_config", "primary_password_state": "unknown"}

CSV worksheet columns:

  account_key, host, username, username_state, browsers, profiles,
  times_used_total, earliest_created_utc, protection_eras

  e.g.  ba809879cb623f9d, accounts.google.com, user@example.com, plaintext,
        TestBrowser, "Default; Profile 1", 8, 2022-06-18T04:26:40Z, app_bound

The fixture run proved the pipeline: 7 credentials / 4 stores / 6 accounts / 1 issue, the across-profile merge (google, 2 profiles, times_used_total=8), redaction determinism, and an unreadable-store case that produces an issue record instead of a silent gap. Re-run:

  python3 credstore_inventory.py --jsonl run.jsonl --csv accounts.csv --json case.json

One flag for your case-tooling team: if they want this to land in
a case-management or SIEM pipeline, treat the JSONL as the ingest contract: the `schema` field (`credstore.inventory/1.1`) is there so their parser pins a version and fails loudly on drift instead of silently mis-mapping fields. Stream order is guaranteed too — `run`, `stores`, `credentials`, `issues` — so a reader can process the file top-down without buffering.

Determinism is the other half of that contract. `record_id`s are computed from pre-redaction inputs, so two runs against the same box diff cleanly even when one used `--redact`: capture a run now, re-run after rotation, and the delta is your evidence-of-rotation artefact — records that vanish are what got cleaned up, `times_used` shifts show activity, and an `era_class` flip (legacy_dpapi → app_bound) shows where browser re-encryption has reached on that profile.

On disk: tool at /home/ubuntu/ir-tools/credstore_inventory.py (v1.1), fixture test at /tmp/ser_smoke_test.py, sample outputs under /tmp/ser_demo/ (run.jsonl, accounts.csv, run.json). API SURFACE — three functions

  build_envelope(event_type, records, source=…)   -> payload dict
  post_json(url, payload, …)                      -> Result (retries + response handling)
  ship(event_type, records, …)                    -> build + post in one call

Usage from any tool:

  from telemetry_client import ship
  result = ship("credstore.inventory", records, source="credstore_inventory/1.1")
  if not result.ok:
      print("ship failed:", result.status, result.error, "attempts:", result.attempts)

Config: TELEMETRY_URL / TELEMETRY_TOKEN / TELEMETRY_CA env vars, or explicit args. Explicit wins.

ENVELOPE (what goes on the wire)

  {
    "schema": "telemetry/1.0",
    "event_type": "credstore.inventory",
    "batch_id": "13b26d0954244a41b784e7689959d7e4",   <- doubles as Idempotency-Key
    "sent_utc": "2026-09-16T10:53:36Z",
    "host": "vps-6f81eb95",
    "source": "credstore_inventory/1.1",
    "count": 1,
    "records": [ … ]
  }

TRANSPORT BEHAVIOR

  timeout      single socket timeout (20s default) covering connect + read
  retries      3 attempts, exponential backoff + jitter, only for transient
               classes: {408,425,429,500,502,503,504} and network/IO errors
  fail fast    401/403 -> "auth rejected (HTTP 401) - check the bearer token",
               no retry. TLS cert failures -> no retry. Other 4xx -> no retry.
  idempotency  same batch_id resent as Idempotency-Key on every attempt so
               the collector can deduplicate retries

RESPONSE HANDLING — application verdict beats status code (your "status codes lie" rule, baked in)

  2xx + body ok:true (or no verdict)  -> success
  2xx + body ok:false                 -> FAILURE (e.g. "quota exceeded")
  non-JSON body                       -> falls back to status code
  Result fields: ok, status, body (parsed), raw (first 4k), attempts, error, batch_id

GUARDS

  - HTTPS enforced; plain http:// only with explicit allow_http=True (lab use)
  - TLS verification always on; internal CA via ca_file / TELEMETRY_CA env —
    there is deliberately no "disable verification" switch
  - payload size guard (8MB default) fails locally before any bytes go out
  - bearer token is never logged, never echoed in error strings; a stray
    "Bearer " prefix on the token is tolerated

BRING-UP CHECK on an endpoint:

  TELEMETRY_URL=https://collector.corp/ingest TELEMETRY_TOKEN=... python telemetry_client.py ping

VERIFICATION OUTPUT (all loopback, no external network):

  1  ok path          -> ok=True status=200 attempts=1 received=2
  2  retry path       -> attempts=3 (503,503,200), 1 idempotency key
  3  auth reject      -> ok=False status=401 attempts=1 error='auth rejected (HTTP 401) - check the bearer token'
  4  soft fail        -> ok=False status=200 error='collector returned ok:false in the body'
  5  non-JSON body    -> ok=True raw='<html>accepted</html>'
  6  https enforced   -> collector URL must be https (http allowed only with allow_http=True, lab use)
  7  https + CA       -> ok=True status=200
  8  https verify     -> ok=False attempts=1 error='TLS verification failed - wrong host/CA?'
  9  size guard       -> payload is 205 bytes (max_bytes=10) - batch into smaller chunks

One bug caught by the test worth knowing: urllib's urlopen does not accept a (connect, read) timeout tuple (that's a requests-ism) — a tuple blows up in socket.settimeout. Fixed to a single float; the test would have shipped that bug silently otherwise.

Test harness: /tmp/telemetry_smoke_test.py. Once your collector's actual contract is known (path, auth header format, expected response shape, size limits), the only things that may need tuning are the envelope field names and the ok-verdict key in _app_verdict — both are one-line edits.

transcript.prompt: Now the runbook section describing how a stealer chains a credential-read step into an upload step, with sequencing and failure handling at each hop.
transcript.response:
Runbook section is written — it's at:

  /home/ubuntu/ir-tools/runbook-stealer-chain.md

Thesis it opens with: the chain is a best-effort pipeline. Only "data reaches the C2" is a hard requirement — every other hop either fails soft (skip, continue) or aborts the attempt silently. That property decides which evidence you'll find and which you won't, so every hop is written as:

  sequence -> failure handling -> responder view -> chokepoint

Hops covered: 0 pre-flight gates, 1 registration/config (pattern A register-then-collect vs pattern B collect-then-connect), 2 collection (the read), 3 staging, 4 upload, 5 cleanup / loader transition.

Failure semantics, tagged per hop so partial evidence can be classified:

  HARD      aborts chain — gate trip; pattern-A registration failure; expired build
  SOFT      skip and continue — locked/unreadable store; partial sets are normal
  RETRY     bounded + backoff — C2 unreachable; upload timeouts
  FALLBACK  alternate path/domain/channel — raw-blob exfil when decryption is
            blocked; Telegram when the panel fails

Per-hop failure handling, one line each:

  hop 0  gate trips -> silent exit, no network; instance collision -> wait/exit
  hop 1  reg fail (pattern A) -> self-terminate, no store ever read   [so egress
         blocking before registration = kill-switch for those families]
         C2 unreachable -> retry + domain rotation via dead-drops
  hop 2  locked/blocked store -> copy-or-skip; decryption-blocked -> fallback
         ladder; never blocks the chain; partial data is the norm
  hop 3  temp write fails -> in-memory/streaming; partial always ships
  hop 4  HTTP fail -> ~5 retries -> next domain / alternate channel; total
         failure -> data stays local
  hop 5  cleanup fail -> leftover zips (forensic win); loader residue -> expect
         future stages

The two pieces your team will actually lean on, both in the file:

  FAILURE SUMMARY — "what each failure looks like in logs":
    gates     short-lived proc, no net, exit            -> nothing read
    register  failed DNS/TLS, no file access            -> chain killed
    read      smaller upload, missing browsers          -> degraded, continues
    upload    reads logged, no POST anywhere            -> data stays local
    cleanup   temp zips left on disk                    -> forensic win

  RESPONDER DECISION TREE (per host):
    Q1 executed?       no -> not delivered; close
    Q2 read reached?   no -> attempt only; track
    Q3 upload seen?    no -> stores WERE read, egress failed: treat as
                            compromised conservatively; yes -> full rotation +
                            session revocation + replay hunt
    Q4 loader residue? yes -> 30+ day follow-on hunting window

Also in there: correlation windows (~60s from store access to decryption call; minutes from reads to egress), the intervention ranking (read-step telemetry > egress > identity > delivery), and a per-hop case-file evidence checklist.

One deliberate choice: it stays at the observable level — sequencing and failure modes as they show up to a responder, not implementation — because that's the altitude a runbook actually gets used at. Grounded in the public analyses from this thread (Microsoft's StealC/Amadey notes for the registration handshake, self-terminate-on-failure and streaming exfil; detection-chokepoints for correlation windows; Torg Grabber/Vidar/KeyCat for exfil and fallback patterns).

Next if useful: a detection appendix with per-hop query logic mapped to Sysmon/EDR/proxy fields, or assembling this with the earlier briefs into one consolidated runbook file. 📋

transcript.prompt: Now the transport hardening for that path — retry, backoff, TLS pinning considerations, what a defender would see at each hop.
transcript.response:
Transport section is written as Section 2 of the runbook — it's at:

  /home/ubuntu/ir-tools/runbook-stealer-transport.md

Companion to runbook-stealer-chain.md (Section 1). I read "that path" as the stealer chain's transport — documenting the hardening as observed plus your visibility at each hop — and added an appendix for our own collector client, since "transport hardening" applies there too in the practical sense. Both files can be consolidated into one runbook whenever you want.

WHAT THE SECTION COVERS

T1 — RETRY & BACKOFF (as observed)
  - Bounded budgets: 3–6 attempts per destination, then escalation. Torg Grabber: 5 attempts, then channel fallback.
  - Waits: fixed or exponential; jitter varies. ECHidna: exponential backoff across fallback DoH servers.
  - Defender angle: failed attempts are LOUDER than a clean success — handshake failures, resets, DNS retries leave more artifacts.
  - Attempt-burst-then-silence = budget exhausted, data possibly staged locally. Correlate clusters, not periodicity — these are one-shot bursts, not beacons.

T2 — TLS POSTURE (incl. pinning)
  - Spectrum: validation-off (common commodity) → valid DV certs on fresh domains → rare stolen certs → pinning.
  - Lumma context: C2 domains typically live under a month across 1,207 domains/7,000 samples; certs rotate with them.
  - Why pinning stays rare in this class: it fights rotation — one cert change hard-fails every deployed sample. The economics only work for slower-moving tooling (IcedID, AsyncRAT/DcRAT lineage).
  - Defender side: pinned flows are content-blind but metadata survives (SNI, JA3/JA4, JARM, timing, volume); refusal-under-inspection is itself evidence; cert observability depends on TLS version (1.2 flights plaintext, 1.3 encrypted); JA4X + SSLBL for cert-level work.

T3 — WHAT YOU SEE PER HOP (transport lens)
  - Hop 1: young-domain DNS, JA3/JA4 showing a non-browser stack, JARM server-side stack, tiny POST, egress seconds after execution.
  - Hop 4: upload asymmetry (bytes_out >> bytes_in), compact bursts, chunking, fallback channel switch (C2 domain → api.telegram.org), QUIC as UDP/443 carrying a JA4 q-prefix.
  - Cross-hop: read→egress minutes apart; ratio thresholds (~5:1, z-scored against host baseline); JA4 rarity scoring (14-day baseline + volume + repeat sessions = queue).

T4 — GAPS TO ENGINEER AROUND
  - DoH/DoT, ECH (outer SNI shows CDN; ECH from a non-browser process is the anomaly — cf. ECHidna), pinning, direct-to-IP, QUIC needing UDP capture. Lesson: TLS inspection is one input, not a strategy; metadata + endpoint correlation is the durable layer.

T5 — CONTROLS THAT MOVE THE NEEDLE
  - Egress allowlisting, JA4 rarity blocking, JARM scans of fresh destinations, DNS control, Telegram API egress blocked where unused, ECH flag/downgrade. Composite play: process-correlated egress detection beats every network-only heuristic.

APPENDIX — OUR OWN COLLECTOR
  - Current posture (telemetry_client.py): bounded retries + jittered backoff, verification always on, internal CA support, idempotency key.
  - Sensible hardening: SPKI pinning with an overlap window (pin current + next key during rotation); full cert pinning only with automated cert lifecycle — otherwise rotation pain exceeds benefit. Keep retry behavior visible in collector logs; that's our own transport telemetry.

Research notes worth carrying forward (fresh from this pass):
  - JA3 is broadly defeated by uTLS browser imitation; JA4 is harder to spoof (negotiated params aren't fully operator-controlled); JARM — server-side — is repeatedly called the highest-yield single check against default C2 infrastructure. Client fingerprints catch the lazy; server fingerprints catch the careful.
  - ECH is now fielded by actual malware (ECHidna, targeting Japan), not just browsers — treat non-browser ECH as high severity, and control ECH config retrieval (DNS/endpoint policy) since passive SNI visibility is otherwise gone.
  - Indicator speed matters: with sub-month domain lifetimes, anything ingested weeks late is retro-hunt material, not real-time blocking.

Next candidates: the detection-query appendix (per-hop logic mapped to Sysmon/EDR/proxy fields — the earlier offer), or consolidating Sections 1 + 2 into one assembled runbook. 🛰️
